nodeData.note: Beginner track · Bias and fairness, privacy (Kenya DPA, GDPR), AI laws around the world, deepfakes, responsible use.

children.note: Why AI can treat people unequally, where that comes from, famous real cases, what it means for African languages and people, and how to test for and reduce bias.
What AI tools do with the data you give them, what Kenya's Data Protection Act 2019 and the EU's GDPR require, and simple habits for using AI safely with work, patient and client information.
A beginner's tour of how the EU, US, China, UK, the African Union and Kenya govern AI, with key dates. Laws change quickly: treat this as a map and always check the current text.
How AI fakes of faces, voices and news are made, how to spot them, how they have been used in elections and scams, and the simple habits that protect you and your organisation.
How to use AI well at work and in life: keep humans in charge, be open about AI use, own the results, count the environmental cost, and set a clear workplace AI policy.

nodeData.note: Why AI can treat people unequally, where that comes from, famous real cases, what it means for African languages and people, and how to test for and reduce bias.

children.note: An AI system is biased when it works noticeably better or worse for some groups of people, or treats them unfairly, in a way that repeats again and again rather than by chance.
Every AI makes errors. Bias is when the errors pile up on the same kind of person, for example one skin tone, gender, accent, age group or region.

manas.q: What makes an AI error a sign of bias rather than bad luck?

children.note: Most AI learns patterns from old examples. If the past was unfair, or some people were missing from the examples, the AI copies that unfairness and can repeat it at huge scale.

Fair can mean equal accuracy for every group, equal chances of a good outcome, or judging each person on their own merits. These goals can clash, so people must choose which matters most for each use.

manas.q: Why can't one AI system satisfy every definition of fairness at once?

children.topic: Why it matters more with AI
children.note: A biased clerk affects the people in front of them. A biased system used by a bank, hospital or government can affect millions of decisions quickly and quietly.
People tend to trust a computer's answer over their own judgement, even when it is wrong. That makes a biased tool look neutral and authoritative.

manas.q: What is automation bias?

children.note: Think of a market scale that reads a little heavy. Each sale looks fine, but over a year some customers have paid much more. Bias in AI works the same way: small, steady and easy to miss.
Bias can enter at every step: what data is collected, how it is labelled, what the system is told to aim for, and where and how it is finally used.
If a face, voice or medical dataset has few examples of some people, the model learns less about them and makes more mistakes on them. This is called under-representation.

manas.q: What is under-representation in training data?

children.note: Records of past hiring, lending or policing reflect past human decisions, including prejudice. A model trained to copy those decisions learns the prejudice too.
Humans tag the training examples. Their own assumptions, language and culture shape the labels, for example which photos count as 'professional' or which comments count as 'offensive'.
Even if a system never sees race or tribe, other details like home area, school or phone type can stand in for them. Removing the sensitive column does not remove the bias.

manas.q: Why doesn't deleting the 'race' or 'gender' column remove bias?

children.note: Designers sometimes measure what is easy rather than what matters, such as past spending instead of real health need. The model then optimises the wrong thing very well.
Sensors and devices can work differently on different bodies, for example light-based sensors on darker skin. Biased measurements then feed biased data into AI.
A model built on data from one country, hospital or language can fail when moved elsewhere. A tool trained on European patients may not fit a clinic in Kisumu or Kolkata.

manas.q: Why can a model that works well in one country fail in another?

children.note: If a model sends more police or loan checks to one area, more problems are recorded there, which seems to prove the model right. The bias feeds itself over time.
Teams that lack people from the affected communities are more likely to miss problems that those communities would spot at once.
Real examples show that bias is not a theory. Each case taught the field something about data, targets and testing.
Joy Buolamwini and Timnit Gebru tested commercial face-analysis tools. Errors in guessing gender were tiny for lighter-skinned men but reached about one in three for darker-skinned women.

manas.q: What did the Gender Shades study find?

children.note: In the United States, several Black men have been wrongly arrested after police relied on facial recognition matches that turned out to be false.
A ProPublica investigation of a US tool that predicts reoffending found that Black defendants who did not reoffend were far more often labelled high risk than white defendants who did not reoffend.

manas.q: What did ProPublica report about the COMPAS tool?

children.note: Amazon built an experimental CV-screening model trained on past hires, who were mostly men. It learned to mark down CVs that mentioned women's activities, and the company dropped it.

manas.q: Why did Amazon's experimental CV screener penalise women?

children.note: A US algorithm used past health spending to pick patients for extra care. Because less was spent on Black patients, they had to be much sicker to get the same score.

manas.q: What went wrong in the 2019 health risk algorithm study?

children.topic: 📄 Dissecting racial bias in an algorithm
children.note: Obermeyer and colleagues, Science 2019: the study that exposed the cost-as-proxy problem and showed that changing the target greatly reduced the bias.
Finger oxygen sensors more often missed dangerously low oxygen in Black patients. Not AI itself, but any AI trained on those readings inherits the error.

manas.q: Why does pulse oximeter bias matter for medical AI?

children.note: Sjoding and colleagues, New England Journal of Medicine 2020: hidden low oxygen was missed about three times as often in Black patients as in white patients.
In 2015 Google Photos labelled photos of Black people with an animal label. The fix was to block the label, which showed how hard the deeper problem was.
Ask some image generators for a 'doctor' or 'CEO' and you may get mostly light-skinned men; ask for 'poor village' and you may get mostly African scenes. They mirror stereotypes in web images.
Africa has well over a thousand languages, yet most AI is built mainly on English and a few rich-world languages. This gap shapes who AI serves well.
AI learns language from huge amounts of online text. Kiswahili has some, but languages like Dholuo, Kalenjin or Kikuyu have very little, so tools handle them poorly.

manas.q: Why do chatbots handle most African languages poorly?

children.note: Languages with little digital data are called low-resource. Translation, speech and safety filters are usually weakest in them, even when millions of people speak them.

manas.q: What is a low-resource language?

children.note: Voice assistants and transcription tools are often trained mostly on American or British voices. Kenyan, Nigerian or Indian English accents can get more errors.
Harmful content and scams written in local languages or Sheng can slip past filters tuned for English, while harmless local phrases may be wrongly blocked.
Skin-condition image collections are dominated by lighter skin. A skin-check app may miss conditions on darker skin, which matters for African patients.
Lending apps that score people from phone and mobile-money data can disadvantage those with older phones, shared phones or less digital history, often women and rural users.
Masakhane is a grassroots research community of African researchers building language tools and datasets for African languages, so the people who speak them shape the technology.

manas.q: What is Masakhane?

children.note: A 2023 preprint describing an open, free machine translation platform for African languages from the Masakhane community.
Some data labelling and content moderation for global AI firms has been done by workers in Kenya and other countries on low pay, raising fairness questions beyond the model itself.
Collecting local data with consent, paying local experts fairly, testing tools on local users, and supporting African-led research all reduce the gap.
Bias cannot be removed by good intentions. It has to be measured, fixed where possible, and watched after launch.
Split test results by gender, age, region, language and skin tone where relevant and lawful. An average accuracy of 95% can hide 70% for one group.

manas.q: Why is a single overall accuracy number not enough?

children.note: Try the tool with the people who will actually use it, in their languages and settings, before rolling it out. A pilot in one county or ward reveals problems early.
Independent reviewers, researchers or regulators can check a system without the builder's blind spots. Gender Shades was an outside audit.
Add more examples of under-represented groups, correct bad labels, and remove features that act as proxies. Better data usually beats clever maths.
Ask whether the model predicts what truly matters. Changing a health tool from 'past cost' to 'actual illness' cut most of the bias in the 2019 study.

children.topic: Keep a human who can say no
children.note: For decisions about jobs, loans, health or freedom, a trained person should review AI suggestions and be free to overrule them.

manas.q: Why keep a human able to overrule high-stakes AI decisions?

children.note: People affected by an automated decision should be able to find out, question it and get a human review. Kenyan and EU data law give rights on this; check the current text.
Bias can appear later as users, prices or populations change. Keep checking results by group and keep a log of complaints.
Free toolkits such as IBM's AI Fairness 360 and Google's Fairness Indicators help technical teams measure bias. They help, but they cannot decide what is fair for you.
No AI is perfectly fair, and some fixes create new problems. Knowing the limits keeps expectations honest.
A common mistake. AI reflects the data and choices of the people who built it, so it is never automatically neutral.

manas.q: Is AI automatically neutral because it is a machine?

children.note: You can reduce and manage bias, but some trade-offs remain. Be clear which groups and harms you tested for and which you did not.
Clumsy fixes, like forcing diversity into every generated image, can produce false or offensive results, such as historically wrong pictures.
If good data does not exist for the people affected, or a wrong decision would be grave, the fairest choice may be not to automate at all.
Who decides, who benefits and who can complain are human questions. Involve the affected community, not just engineers.
Short videos that explain AI bias with real examples.
A clear 11-minute tour of the types of bias and how they enter AI systems.
IBM explains what algorithmic bias is and practical ways teams reduce it.
Joy Buolamwini's talk on the 'coded gaze' and why face tools failed on her face.
A five-minute summary of the audit that measured error gaps in face analysis.
A short beginner explanation of how biased data leads to biased programs.
Trusted places to go deeper.
Overview of causes, cases and laws, with many links to original reporting.
The different mathematical definitions of fairness and why they conflict.
The original 2018 audit paper by Buolamwini and Gebru.
A free online book on fairness for readers who want more depth.
A free beginner course that includes the societal side of AI.

nodeData.note: What AI tools do with the data you give them, what Kenya's Data Protection Act 2019 and the EU's GDPR require, and simple habits for using AI safely with work, patient and client information.

children.note: AI tools run on data, and much of it is about people. Knowing what counts as personal data is the first step to using AI without harming anyone.
Any information that can identify a living person, directly or with other details: name, ID number, phone, photo, voice, location, or even a unique mix of age, village and job.

manas.q: What is personal data?

children.note: Extra-risky categories such as health, genetic and biometric data, ethnic origin, religion and sex life. Laws in Kenya and the EU demand stronger care for these.

manas.q: Name three kinds of sensitive personal data.

children.note: Fingerprints, face scans, iris scans and voiceprints. Unlike a password, you cannot change your face if it leaks, so it deserves the most protection.
Text you paste into an online AI tool leaves your control. It may be stored, read by staff or used for training, and deleting it later is not always possible.
Pasting data into a public chatbot is like photocopying a file at a busy shop: the shop may keep a copy, and you cannot be sure who sees it.

children.topic: What AI tools do with data
children.note: Each provider has its own rules, and they change. These are the common patterns to check before typing anything private.
Most chatbots keep conversation history on their servers, often for weeks or longer, for safety checks, legal reasons and to show you past chats.

manas.q: Are chatbot conversations usually kept on the provider's servers?

children.note: Some free consumer services may use your chats to improve future models unless you switch this off. Business and enterprise plans usually promise not to train on your data. Check the settings and terms.

manas.q: Why do business AI plans differ from free consumer plans on privacy?

children.note: Providers may have staff or contractors review samples of conversations to improve quality or catch abuse.
Some assistants remember facts about you across chats. Useful, but it means more personal details are stored. You can usually view and delete these memories.

children.topic: Models can leak what they learned
children.note: Large models have sometimes repeated pieces of their training text word for word, including personal details found online. This is called memorisation.
Your data may be processed in another country. Data laws, including Kenya's, put conditions on sending personal data abroad.

manas.q: Why does it matter which country an AI provider stores data in?

children.note: When an AI can read your email, files or calendar, it touches far more personal data. Give it access only to what the task needs.
Some AI firms built training sets by collecting public web pages and photos without asking. Regulators in several countries have challenged this.
Kenya's main privacy law. It puts the constitutional right to privacy into practice and applies to anyone handling personal data of people in Kenya. Check the current text for details.
Article 31 of the Constitution of Kenya 2010 gives every person the right to privacy. The Data Protection Act 2019 turns that right into detailed rules.

manas.q: Which article of Kenya's Constitution gives the right to privacy?

children.note: The Act created the Office of the Data Protection Commissioner (ODPC). It registers data handlers, takes complaints, investigates and can issue penalties.

manas.q: What does the ODPC do?

children.note: A data controller decides why and how data is used, for example a clinic. A processor handles data for them, such as an AI or cloud provider. Both have duties.

manas.q: What is the difference between a data controller and a processor?

children.note: Many organisations that handle personal data, especially in health, education and finance, must register with the ODPC. Check the regulations for whether yours must.
Use data lawfully and fairly, only for a clear purpose, collect no more than needed, keep it accurate and secure, and do not keep it longer than necessary.
People can be told how their data is used, see it, correct it, object to some uses and ask for deletion. There are also protections against purely automated decisions.
Before high-risk processing, such as new AI that profiles people or uses health data at scale, a data protection impact assessment is expected.

manas.q: When should a Kenyan organisation do a data protection impact assessment?

children.note: If personal data leaks, the controller must tell the Data Commissioner within 72 hours of learning of it, and inform affected people where there is real risk.

manas.q: How fast must a breach be reported to Kenya's Data Commissioner?

children.note: The ODPC can fine up to five million shillings or 1% of annual turnover, whichever is lower, and courts can order compensation. Figures may change; check the current text.
In 2023 Kenya suspended the Worldcoin eye-scanning project over privacy and security concerns, and in May 2025 it was ordered to delete biometric data collected in Kenya.

manas.q: What happened with Worldcoin's iris scanning in Kenya?

children.note: The EU's General Data Protection Regulation is the world's most influential privacy law and a model for many others, including parts of Kenya's.
Adopted in 2016 and in force since 25 May 2018. It applies to organisations outside the EU too if they offer services to, or monitor, people in the EU.

manas.q: When did the GDPR start to apply?

children.topic: A legal basis for every use
children.note: You need a lawful reason to use personal data, such as consent, a contract, a legal duty or a legitimate interest that does not override people's rights.
Access, correction, deletion (the 'right to be forgotten'), data portability and objection. Kenyan law shares many of these ideas.
People have rights when important decisions about them are made only by automated means, including asking for human involvement. Check the current text for limits.

manas.q: What GDPR protection relates to purely automated decisions?

children.note: Serious breaches can be fined up to 20 million euros or 4% of worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher.
In 2023 Italy's privacy regulator briefly blocked ChatGPT over data concerns until changes were made, showing GDPR applies to AI chatbots.
The UK has its own 'UK GDPR'. Brazil, South Africa, India and many others have comparable laws. Check which apply to you.
Most AI privacy accidents at work are simple: someone pastes the wrong thing into the wrong tool. A few habits prevent most of them.
Before pasting, ask: would I be comfortable if this text appeared in tomorrow's newspaper? If not, do not put it into an unapproved AI tool.

manas.q: What is the 'newspaper test' for AI prompts?

children.note: Samsung engineers pasted confidential source code and meeting notes into a public chatbot. The company then restricted staff use of such tools.

manas.q: What lesson does the 2023 Samsung chatbot incident teach?

children.note: Use the AI tools your employer has approved and set up, usually business plans with data protections, not personal free accounts.
Replace names, ID numbers, phone numbers and account numbers with placeholders like [Client A] before asking for help with a document.
Turn off training on your chats where the option exists, and review saved memories and chat history from time to time.
Never paste passwords, API keys, bank details, M-Pesa PINs or ID scans into a chatbot, even to 'check' them.
AI note-takers record and transcribe everyone. Tell participants, get agreement, and do not use them for confidential or HR conversations.
AI-written text can include private details from your prompt. Read outputs before sharing them outside your team.
Doctors, lawyers, accountants, HR staff and NGOs hold some of the most sensitive data there is. AI can help them, but only with extra care.
Under Kenyan and EU law, health data is a special category with stricter rules. A careless prompt can be a legal breach as well as an ethical one.

manas.q: Why does health data need extra care with AI tools?

children.note: Do not paste identifiable patient or client records into free public AI tools. Use systems your organisation has approved, with a proper agreement in place.

children.topic: De-identifying is harder than it looks
children.note: Removing the name is not enough. Age, ward, rare condition and date of visit together can identify someone in a small community.

manas.q: Why is deleting the name not enough to anonymise a patient record?

children.note: Tell patients or clients when AI is used with their data, for example an AI scribe in a consultation, and respect a refusal.
If an AI draft of a discharge summary or legal letter contains an error, the professional who signs it is responsible. Always check it.
Before buying an AI product, ask where data is stored, who can access it, whether it trains on your data, and how breaches are reported. Get it in writing.

A 2025 npj Digital Medicine commentary on ways to protect electronic health records when using large language models, such as local models, synthetic data, differential privacy, federated learning and de-identification.

children.topic: 📄 Patient privacy and LLMs: a review
children.note: A 2025 scoping review in the Journal of Medical Internet Research on how well current approaches protect patient information.
Short videos on AI, privacy and data protection law.

children.topic: ▶ What NOT to share with AI
children.note: A two-minute guide to the kinds of information to keep out of chatbots.
365 Data Science: how AI tools collect and use data, explained for beginners.
IBM Technology: how AI systems can leak data and what organisations do about it.
Wall Street Journal: a three-minute overview of the EU's data protection law.
Kenya's data protection regulator discusses the law and how it works in practice.
Official and trusted sources.

children.topic: Office of the Data Protection Commissioner
children.note: Kenya's regulator: the Act, regulations, guidance, registration and complaints.
Plain overview of the GDPR, its history and global influence.
IAPP article on the difference between truly anonymous and merely masked data.
A free beginner course covering AI and its effects on society.

nodeData.note: A beginner's tour of how the EU, US, China, UK, the African Union and Kenya govern AI, with key dates. Laws change quickly: treat this as a map and always check the current text.

children.topic: Why and how AI is regulated
children.note: Governments regulate AI to protect safety, rights and fair markets while still allowing useful innovation. Laws change fast, so always check the current text.
A common summary: the US leans on markets and existing laws, China on state control, and the EU on protecting individual rights. Most countries mix these.

manas.q: How are the US, China and EU approaches to AI often summarised?

children.note: Many rules scale with risk: a spam filter needs little oversight, while AI that decides loans, jobs or medical care needs much more.

manas.q: What does a risk-based approach to AI regulation mean?

children.note: Data protection, consumer, anti-discrimination, medical device and copyright laws already cover many AI uses, even where no AI-specific law exists.
A law is binding and enforceable. Strategies, principles and codes of practice guide behaviour but usually carry no direct penalty.
Among the first intergovernmental AI principles, calling for AI that respects human rights, is transparent and has clear accountability.
UNESCO member states adopted a global Recommendation on the Ethics of AI in November 2021. It guides national policy but is not a binding law.
Regulation (EU) 2024/1689: the first broad AI law of a major economy. It sorts AI uses by risk and phases in duties over several years. Check the current text.
Proposed April 2021, approved by Parliament on 13 March 2024 and by the Council on 21 May 2024, in force on 1 August 2024.

manas.q: When did the EU AI Act enter into force?

children.note: Bans applied after 6 months (February 2025), general-purpose AI duties after 12 months (August 2025), most rules after 24 months, some high-risk duties after 36. Dates may be adjusted; check.

manas.q: Roughly how long after entry into force did the EU AI Act's bans apply?

children.note: Uses seen as a clear threat to rights are banned, such as social scoring by authorities and manipulative AI that exploits vulnerable people.

manas.q: Give one example of AI banned under the EU AI Act.

children.note: AI in areas like hiring, education, credit, essential services, medical devices and law enforcement must meet strict rules on data quality, documentation, human oversight and accuracy.

manas.q: Name two areas where AI counts as high risk under the EU AI Act.

children.note: Mainly transparency duties: people should know when they are talking to a chatbot, and AI-generated or deepfake content should be labelled.
Most everyday AI, like spam filters or game AI, has no new obligations under the Act.
Providers of large models like those behind chatbots must share technical information and respect copyright rules. The most powerful models face extra safety evaluation.
A voluntary General-Purpose AI Code of Practice was published on 10 July 2025 to help model providers show they comply.
Breaking the bans can cost up to 35 million euros or 7% of worldwide turnover, whichever is higher. Lower ceilings apply to other breaches.

manas.q: What is the maximum fine for using banned AI under the EU AI Act?

children.note: The Act gives duties both to providers, who build or sell AI systems, and to deployers, the organisations that use them at work. A hospital using a high-risk tool is a deployer.

manas.q: Under the EU AI Act, what is a deployer?

children.note: Since February 2025, organisations that provide or use AI systems must take steps so their staff have enough understanding of AI for their role.
A Kenyan or Indian company whose AI is used in the EU can be covered. Exporters and outsourcing firms should check whether it applies to them.
Two very different models: the US has no single federal AI law, while China has a series of specific, binding rules.

children.topic: US: no single federal AI law
children.note: The US relies on existing laws, agency rules, state laws and presidential executive orders, which can change when administrations change.

manas.q: Does the United States have one comprehensive federal AI law?

children.note: A broad AI safety executive order of October 2023 was revoked in January 2025. In December 2025 a new order sought to limit state AI laws. Check the current position.

children.topic: US: NIST AI Risk Management Framework
children.note: A voluntary guide from the US standards agency, released in 2023, that helps organisations map, measure and manage AI risks. Widely used worldwide.

children.topic: US: states act on their own
children.note: States such as Colorado and California have passed their own AI laws, for example Colorado's 2024 law on high-risk AI and discrimination. Start dates have shifted; check.
After a fake Biden voice robocall in January 2024, the US communications regulator ruled in February 2024 that AI-generated voices in robocalls fall under existing restrictions.
China's 2017 national plan set AI goals to 2030. Rules on recommendation algorithms (2022) and deepfakes, called deep synthesis (January 2023), followed.

manas.q: When did China's deep synthesis (deepfake) rules take effect?

children.note: China's Interim Measures for generative AI services took effect on 15 August 2023, covering content, data and labelling for services offered to the public.

manas.q: When did China's generative AI measures come into force?

children.note: Providers must file algorithms with the Cyberspace Administration of China. Rules issued in 2025 require visible labels and hidden metadata on AI-generated content.
The UK chose a lighter, regulator-led approach, and several international agreements try to set shared ground rules.
A March 2023 white paper set general AI principles and asked existing regulators, such as those for finance or health, to apply them in their sectors.

manas.q: How does the UK mainly regulate AI?

children.note: AI that uses personal data in the UK must follow UK data protection law, enforced by the Information Commissioner's Office.
The UK hosted the first global AI Safety Summit at Bletchley Park. Countries signed the Bletchley Declaration on risks from frontier AI.

manas.q: What was signed at Bletchley Park in November 2023?

children.note: Created at the 2023 summit to test the safety of the most advanced AI models. Similar institutes were set up in other countries.
The first international treaty on AI and human rights, signed in Vilnius on 5 September 2024. It binds only countries that ratify it.

manas.q: What is the Council of Europe Framework Convention on AI?

children.note: Africa is building its own AI governance, with emphasis on development, data rights and African values. Most measures are strategies and data laws rather than AI-specific statutes.
The African Union adopted a Continental AI Strategy in 2024 to guide member states on AI for development, skills, data and ethical safeguards.

manas.q: When did the African Union adopt its Continental AI Strategy?

children.note: The AU Convention on Cyber Security and Personal Data Protection, adopted in Malabo in 2014, set shared principles for data protection across Africa. Check which countries have ratified.
The African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights has studied AI and human rights and supports an African treaty on AI, stressing collective rights and values like Ubuntu.
Over thirty African countries have data protection laws, which already govern much AI use, for example Kenya, Nigeria, South Africa and Rwanda. Check each country's text.
Kenya's main tool for AI governance today. It covers personal data, profiling and automated decisions, enforced by the ODPC.

manas.q: Which Kenyan law currently does most to govern AI use?

children.topic: Kenya: Computer Misuse and Cybercrimes Act 2018
children.note: Covers offences like unauthorised access, false publications and cyber harassment, which can apply to AI-made fakes and scams. Parts have been challenged in court; check.
Kenya's ICT ministry published a national AI strategy for 2025 to 2030 on infrastructure, data, skills, research and governance. It is a strategy, not a law; check the current text.

manas.q: Is Kenya's AI Strategy 2025–2030 a binding law?

children.note: Rwanda adopted a national AI policy in 2023, and countries including Nigeria, Egypt and South Africa have strategies or drafts. Status changes often; check.
You do not need to be a lawyer to stay safe. A few steps tell you which rules matter for your work.
Ask: where are we based, where are our users, and what data do we use? A Nairobi clinic with EU patients may face Kenyan and EU rules.

manas.q: What three questions help decide which AI laws apply to you?

children.note: Keep a simple register of AI tools in use, what they do, what data they touch and who is responsible for each one.
Hiring, credit, health and policing uses need far more care than drafting emails. Borrow the EU's four tiers as a simple guide even if you are not in Europe.
Summaries and videos go out of date. Check the official text from the regulator or official journal before making decisions.
Put a reminder every six months to check for new rules or changed dates in the places you operate. AI law is moving fast.
For high-risk or cross-border AI, talk to a qualified lawyer or data protection officer. This map is a guide, not legal advice.

children.topic: Myth: no AI law, no rules
children.note: Wrong. Data, consumer, employment and professional laws already apply to AI everywhere.

manas.q: If a country has no AI-specific law, can you use AI however you like?

children.note: Changes in AI rules during 2026, checked on Wikipedia in October 2026. Always confirm with the official text.

The bulk of the AI Act, including the Article 50 transparency duties such as labelling deepfakes and telling people they talk to a chatbot, applies from 2 August 2026. Some high-risk duties come in August 2027; check for changes.

manas.q: When did most EU AI Act duties, including transparency, start to apply?

children.note: India still has no standalone AI law, but amended IT Rules notified on 10 February 2026 and in force from 20 February 2026 set rules for synthetically generated content. Check the current text.

manas.q: How did India regulate AI-made content in 2026?

children.note: Passed in December 2024, it makes businesses that build or use generative AI responsible for safety and transparency, including risk assessments. Check its start dates.
After Bletchley (2023), Seoul (2024) and Paris (2025), the next global AI summit was held in New Delhi in February 2026, the first in the Global South.

manas.q: Where was the 2026 global AI summit held?

children.note: The first session of the UN Global Dialogue on AI Governance took place in Geneva in July 2026, a forum for all countries to discuss shared AI rules.
In late September 2026, leaders of 20 countries and the EU signed a non-binding declaration on keeping AI under human control, common safety standards and incident reporting.
Videos on AI laws and governance.
EU Made Simple explains the risk tiers and goals of the EU AI Act in five minutes.
IBM Technology on why organisations need AI governance and how to start.
IBM Technology walks through the US voluntary framework for managing AI risk.
Mind Foundry compares how major jurisdictions are approaching AI rules.
A CSIS panel examines the AU Continental AI Strategy and the African AI landscape.
Official texts and overviews.
Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 in the EU's official journal.
A country-by-country overview that is updated often.
History, tiers, timeline and criticism of the EU AI Act.
Kenya's data protection regulator, the main enforcer of rules touching AI and personal data.

nodeData.note: How AI fakes of faces, voices and news are made, how to spot them, how they have been used in elections and scams, and the simple habits that protect you and your organisation.

children.note: Deepfakes are images, videos or audio made or changed with AI so that people appear to say or do things they never did. Faking media is old; AI makes it cheap, fast and convincing.
A blend of 'deep learning', the AI method behind them, and 'fake'. The word spread from around 2017.

manas.q: Where does the word 'deepfake' come from?

children.note: The wider family of AI-made content: generated photos, cloned voices, AI avatars and fake documents. Not all of it is harmful; films and dubbing use it legitimately.
Misinformation is false content shared by mistake. Disinformation is false content spread on purpose to deceive. Deepfakes can be either once they spread.

manas.q: What is the difference between misinformation and disinformation?

children.note: Simple tricks without advanced AI, like a real video slowed down, cropped or given a false caption. Often just as effective as deepfakes.
Dubbing films into Kiswahili or Hindi, restoring a voice for someone who lost theirs, or training simulations are legitimate uses when people consent.
When fakes are common, real evidence can be dismissed as 'just AI'. Dishonest people benefit from the doubt itself.

manas.q: What is the 'liar's dividend'?

children.note: You do not need to understand the maths, but knowing the basic recipe helps you see why some fakes slip and others look perfect.
Software studies many photos or video frames of a person, learns their face, then paints it onto another person's face frame by frame.
One early method, the GAN, pits a forger network against a checker network until the forgeries fool the checker. Newer tools use diffusion models.

manas.q: In a GAN, what do the two competing networks do?

children.note: Modern tools can copy a voice from a short recording, such as a voice note or a video clip, then say anything in that voice.

manas.q: How much audio can modern voice cloning need?

children.note: New video generators create whole scenes from a text prompt, and lip-sync tools make a real person's mouth match new words.
Better models, more online photos and voice clips to learn from, and cheaper computing all arrived together after about 2022.
What once needed experts and powerful computers can now be done with free apps or websites, which is why fakes have multiplied.
Chatbots can write thousands of fake news stories, comments or reviews in many languages, including Kiswahili, in minutes.
No single trick works every time, and fakes keep improving. Combine looking closely with checking the source.
Who posted it first? Is it from a known news outlet or official account? An unknown forwarder on WhatsApp is a warning sign.

manas.q: What is the first thing to check about a suspicious video?

children.note: Odd hands or teeth, blurry edges around the face, earrings that change, strange text in the background, and lighting that does not match.
Flat emotion, odd breathing, strange pauses, or a voice that does not fit the room's echo can betray cloned audio.
Search the image or a video frame with tools like Google Lens or TinEye to find where it first appeared or the original version.
Look for checks from established fact-checking groups, including African ones such as Africa Check and PesaCheck.

manas.q: Name two African fact-checking organisations.

children.note: An industry standard that attaches tamper-evident information to a file showing how it was made and edited. Missing credentials prove nothing, but present ones help.

manas.q: What are Content Credentials (C2PA)?

children.note: Some AI companies hide invisible watermarks in generated images or audio. They help, but can sometimes be stripped, and not all tools use them.
Studies show ordinary people often fail to tell good deepfakes from real videos. Detection software also makes mistakes, so check the source too.

manas.q: Can most people reliably spot good deepfakes by eye?

children.topic: 📄 Deepfake detection by humans and machines
children.note: A 2022 PNAS study with over 15,000 participants comparing ordinary viewers and a leading detection model.
Strong emotion, like anger or shock, is a red flag. Wait, check, and if unsure, do not forward.
Deepfakes and AI-written propaganda have appeared in elections worldwide. Even when not decisive, they spread confusion and distrust.
Before the January 2024 New Hampshire primary, thousands of voters got calls with an AI-cloned Biden voice telling them not to vote. The organiser faced charges and fines.

manas.q: What happened in the 2024 New Hampshire robocall case?

children.note: Days before Slovakia's 2023 election, a fake audio clip appeared to capture a party leader discussing vote rigging.
A deepfake video falsely showed Moldova's president backing a pro-Russian party. Officials blamed a foreign influence campaign.
Kenyan and other African elections have seen doctored images, fake polls and false news spread on WhatsApp, X and TikTok. AI makes such content faster to produce.
Beyond video, AI can write thousands of posts for fake accounts that make a fringe view look popular. This is called astroturfing.

manas.q: What is astroturfing?

children.note: Fakes released just before voting leave little time to debunk them before people vote.
Some platforms label AI content, and laws like the EU AI Act require deepfakes to be disclosed. Rules differ by country; check the current text.
Criminals use deepfakes for fraud and abuse. These harms hit ordinary people and businesses, not just politicians.

children.topic: Fake boss on a video call
children.note: In 2024 an employee of the engineering firm Arup in Hong Kong was tricked into sending about 25 million US dollars after a video call with deepfaked senior colleagues.

manas.q: What was the 2024 Arup deepfake scam?

children.note: Scammers clone a child's or relative's voice and call asking for urgent money, for example to M-Pesa, for an accident, arrest or hospital bill.

manas.q: How do voice-cloning family emergency scams work?

children.note: Deepfake videos of famous business people, presidents or news anchors promoting 'get rich' investment schemes circulate widely, including in Kenya.
AI is used to create sexual images of real people without consent, mostly targeting women and girls. It is abuse and often a crime.

manas.q: Who are most often targeted by fake intimate images?

children.note: Scammers use AI photos and polished AI-written messages to build fake profiles for romance scams or overseas job offers that ask for fees.
Fake faces and voices can try to pass online ID checks for bank or SIM registration. Organisations are adding stronger liveness checks.
In Kenya, report fraud to your bank or mobile-money provider at once and to the police; report abusive images to the platform. Keep screenshots as evidence.
Simple habits and processes defeat most deepfake scams, because they rely on rushing you.
Choose a secret word or question with family. If a caller claims to be a relative in trouble, ask for it.

manas.q: What is a family safe word for?

children.note: If a call or message asks for money or secrets, end it and call the person back on a number you already know.

manas.q: What should you do if a familiar voice urgently asks for money?

children.note: In organisations, require two people and a second channel to approve unusual or urgent payments, whoever seems to be asking.
Show staff real examples of cloned voices and fake videos so they know how convincing they are.
Before forwarding a shocking clip to a family or work WhatsApp group, check it. Every forward makes a fake look more believable.

manas.q: Why does forwarding matter even if you did not make the fake?

children.note: Long public voice and video clips make cloning easier. Consider privacy settings for family videos.
Turn on two-step verification for email, banking and social accounts so a cloned voice or fake message alone cannot take them over.
Know who will verify, who will speak publicly and how to request takedowns if a fake of your leader or brand appears.
If your organisation uses AI images or voices, say so clearly. It builds trust and is increasingly a legal duty.

NOVA explains the science of spotting AI-generated faces and video.
NBC News shows how deepfakes are built and how detection tries to keep up.
New Scientist gives practical clues for checking images and videos.
Al Jazeera's Start Here explains why deepfakes are dangerous.
Starling Bank explains how a family safe phrase protects against cloned-voice scams.
Trusted background reading.
History, techniques, harms and responses.
Cases of AI use in election campaigns around the world.
The coalition promoting Content Credentials for media provenance.
A free tool to check whether an image carries Content Credentials.

nodeData.note: How to use AI well at work and in life: keep humans in charge, be open about AI use, own the results, count the environmental cost, and set a clear workplace AI policy.

children.note: Using AI responsibly means getting its benefits while staying in control, being honest about its use, owning the results, and limiting harm to people and the planet.
Most frameworks share the same ideas: human oversight, transparency, accountability, fairness, privacy, safety and sustainability.

manas.q: Name four principles shared by most responsible AI frameworks.

children.note: AI predicts likely words or patterns. It has no judgement, values or responsibility of its own, so those must come from people.

manas.q: Why can't responsibility be handed to the AI itself?

children.note: It cannot guarantee facts, understand your local context fully, know what happened after its training data, or take legal or moral responsibility.
Drafting a party invitation needs little care. A diagnosis, loan decision or court document needs a lot. Match your checks to the harm a mistake could cause.

manas.q: How should the level of checking relate to the task?

children.note: Treat AI like a fast, well-read intern who sometimes makes things up confidently. Useful, but you check the work before it leaves the office.
A capable person must stay in charge of important decisions, understand what the AI is doing, and be able to stop or overrule it.
A person reviews and approves each AI output before it is used, for example a doctor checking an AI-drafted referral letter.

manas.q: What does 'human in the loop' mean?

children.note: The AI acts on its own, but a person monitors it and can step in, for example watching an automated fraud filter.
Chatbots can invent facts, quotes, statistics and references that sound real. Verify anything that matters against a trusted source.

manas.q: What is an AI hallucination?

children.note: In 2023 New York lawyers were fined after filing a brief with court cases invented by ChatGPT. Similar cases have followed in other countries.

manas.q: What happened when lawyers filed AI-invented cases in 2023?

children.note: If reviewers approve hundreds of AI suggestions a day without real checks, oversight exists only on paper. Give them time and authority.
If staff rely on AI for everything, they may lose the skill to spot its errors. Keep practising core tasks without it.
AI agents that can send emails, make payments or change files need clear limits, approval steps and an easy off switch.
Be open about when and how AI is used, so people can trust the work and question decisions that affect them.
Let customers know when they are chatting with a bot, and tell patients or clients when AI helps with their case.

manas.q: Why tell customers when they are chatting with an AI?

children.note: Mark AI-generated images, voices and videos, especially anything realistic. The EU AI Act and Chinese rules already require labels in many cases.
Tell your manager, teacher or editor when AI substantially helped write a report or assignment, following your organisation's rules.
People affected by an AI-assisted decision should get a plain explanation of the main reasons and a way to challenge it.

manas.q: What should someone affected by an AI-assisted decision be able to get?

children.note: Documents from AI makers that describe what a model is for, how it was tested and its known limits. Read them before choosing a tool.
Many AI models cannot fully explain how they reach an answer. For high-stakes uses, prefer tools whose results can be checked or explained.
Someone must own every AI system: its choice, its use and its mistakes. 'The computer did it' is never an acceptable answer.
Each AI tool in use should have a named person responsible for how it is used, monitored and retired.

manas.q: Who should be responsible for an AI tool in an organisation?

children.topic: You sign it, you own it
children.note: A doctor, lawyer, accountant or manager who uses AI output is professionally responsible for it, just as for work done by an assistant.
Record which tool and version was used for important work, and keep logs of decisions so problems can be traced later.
Create a simple way for staff to report AI mistakes or near-misses, then fix the cause, not just the single error.
Contracts with AI suppliers should cover accuracy, data use, security, support and who pays if things go wrong.

children.topic: Give people a route to complain
children.note: Customers and staff need a clear way to question an AI-assisted decision and reach a human.
AI runs in data centres that use electricity, water and hardware. Each chat uses a little; billions of uses add up.
Training and running large models needs a lot of electricity. Data centre energy demand has been rising quickly as AI use grows.

manas.q: Why does AI use electricity?

children.note: Many data centres use water to keep computers cool, which matters in dry areas. How much depends on climate and cooling design.

manas.q: Why do data centres use water?

children.note: AI chips are made with mined materials and are replaced often, adding to electronic waste.

manas.q: Besides energy and water, what environmental cost does AI hardware create?

children.note: A 2024 Nature Computational Science study estimating how much electronic waste generative AI could produce and how to reduce it.
Estimates vary widely because companies report differently and it depends on the model, hardware and local power source. Be wary of precise-sounding numbers.
The same AI task has a smaller footprint on renewable power. Kenya's grid is largely geothermal and hydro, which some data centre projects cite as an advantage.
Choose smaller or faster models for simple jobs, avoid generating dozens of images or videos for fun at work, and do not use AI where a quick search does.
AI is used to improve weather forecasts, manage power grids and track deforestation. Weigh its costs against real benefits.
A short, clear policy helps staff use AI confidently and safely. Use these points as a starting checklist and adapt them to your sector and law.
List which AI tools staff may use, with which accounts, and how to request a new one.

manas.q: What is the first item on a workplace AI policy checklist?

children.note: State plainly what must never go into AI tools: personal, patient, client, financial and confidential data, unless the tool is approved for it.
Give examples of good uses, such as drafting and summarising, and banned ones, such as final medical, hiring or credit decisions without human review.
Require people to verify facts, figures and references before AI-assisted work is sent or published.
Say when staff must tell colleagues, clients or the public that AI was used.
For any AI that affects people, require testing for bias across relevant groups before and after launch.
Map the laws that apply, such as Kenya's Data Protection Act 2019 and, where relevant, the EU AI Act. Check the current text.
Train all staff on the policy, AI limits, privacy and scams, with refreshers as tools change.

manas.q: Why should an AI policy include staff training?

children.note: Name who owns the policy and each tool, and how to report AI mistakes or data leaks.
Review the policy at least once a year, or sooner when tools or laws change.

nodeData.note: Technical track · Linear algebra, probability and statistics, calculus and optimisation — just what AI needs.

children.note: Linear algebra is the maths of lists and grids of numbers. Almost everything an AI model stores and computes, from word meanings to neural network layers, is written as vectors and matrices, so this is the first maths to get comfortable with.

AI works with uncertain, noisy data and gives answers that are guesses with some chance of being wrong. Probability is the language for that uncertainty, and statistics is how we learn from data and judge how much to trust the result.
Training an AI model means nudging millions of numbers so that its errors shrink. Calculus tells you which way to nudge each number, and optimisation is the step-by-step process of doing it.

nodeData.note: Linear algebra is the maths of lists and grids of numbers. Almost everything an AI model stores and computes, from word meanings to neural network layers, is written as vectors and matrices, so this is the first maths to get comfortable with.

children.note: Before matrices, start with the vector: an ordered list of numbers that can describe anything measurable.
A scalar is one number, a vector is a 1-D list, a matrix is a 2-D grid, and a tensor is the general name for arrays with any number of axes. Deep learning libraries call all of them tensors.

manas.q: What is the difference between a scalar, vector, matrix and tensor?

children.topic: A vector is an ordered list
children.note: A vector such as [3, 1, 4] holds numbers in a fixed order, and position matters: the first entry always means the same feature. Example: a patient could be [age, weight, blood pressure].

manas.q: What is a vector, in AI terms?

children.note: In 2-D or 3-D you can draw a vector as an arrow from the origin. Its direction tells you which way it points and its length tells you how big it is. The same ideas carry over to 1,000 dimensions, even though we cannot draw them.
A vector with n numbers lives in n-dimensional space. A grayscale 28×28 image flattened into one list is a 784-dimensional vector.

manas.q: How many dimensions does a flattened 28×28 grayscale image have?

children.note: Add two vectors entry by entry: [1, 2] + [3, 4] = [4, 6]. Multiply by a number to stretch it: 2 × [1, 2] = [2, 4]. "Linear" means built only from these two moves.
The usual length is the square root of the sum of squares: ||v|| = √(v1² + v2² + … + vn²). For [3, 4] the length is 5. Norms also measure how big model weights are.

manas.q: What is the length (L2 norm) of the vector [3, 4]?

children.note: Dividing a vector by its own length gives a unit vector of length 1 that keeps the direction. Normalising lets you compare directions without size getting in the way.
The dot product turns two vectors into one number that says how much they point the same way. It is the single most common operation in AI.
Multiply matching entries and add them up: a·b = a1b1 + a2b2 + … + anbn. Example: [1, 2, 3]·[4, 5, 6] = 4 + 10 + 18 = 32. Both vectors must have the same length.
The dot product also equals |a| × |b| × cos θ, where θ is the angle between the arrows. So it combines how long the vectors are with how closely they line up.
A positive dot product means the vectors point roughly the same way, zero means they are at right angles, and negative means they point in opposite directions.
Two vectors are orthogonal (perpendicular) when their dot product is exactly 0. Orthogonal directions carry completely separate information.

manas.q: What does a dot product of exactly zero tell you?

children.note: Cosine similarity = a·b / (|a| × |b|). It ignores length and keeps only direction, giving a score from −1 to 1. Search engines and chatbots use it to find the text closest in meaning to a question.

manas.q: What does cosine similarity measure, and what is its range?

children.topic: A neuron is a dot product
children.note: An artificial neuron computes y = w·x + b: the dot product of its weights w with the input x, plus a bias b, then passes it through an activation function. Learning means adjusting w and b.

manas.q: What calculation does a single artificial neuron do before its activation function?

children.note: A matrix is a grid of numbers. It can hold a whole dataset, or act as a machine that transforms vectors, which is exactly what a neural network layer does.
A matrix with m rows and n columns has shape m×n. In a dataset, rows are usually examples (patients, farms, sentences) and columns are features.

manas.q: What does the shape m×n of a matrix mean?

children.note: Multiplying a vector by a matrix can rotate, stretch, squash or project it. Thinking of a matrix as a transformation, not just a table, is the key intuition.
Each output entry is the dot product of one matrix row with the vector. A 3×4 matrix turns a 4-number input into a 3-number output.
You can multiply A (m×n) by B (n×p) only when the inner sizes match; the result is m×p. Entry (i, j) of the product is row i of A dotted with column j of B.

manas.q: If A is 32×128 and B is 128×10, what is the shape of AB?

children.note: Matrix multiplication is usually not commutative: AB and BA can differ, or one may not even exist. Applying transformations in a different order gives a different result.

manas.q: Is matrix multiplication commutative?

children.note: The identity matrix I has 1s on the diagonal and leaves vectors unchanged. The transpose Aᵀ swaps rows and columns, turning an m×n matrix into n×m.

manas.q: What does transposing a matrix do?

children.note: A fully connected layer is one matrix-vector product plus a bias vector. Stack many layers with activation functions between them and you have a deep network.
Put a batch of inputs as rows of a matrix X and one multiplication X Wᵀ processes them all together. This is why training works in batches.
In NumPy or PyTorch, write C = A @ B for matrix multiplication. A * B is different: it multiplies entry by entry.
Most early bugs in AI code are linear algebra bugs.
An error like "shapes (3,4) and (3,4) not aligned" means the inner sizes do not match. Print .shape of every array when debugging.
Element-wise (*) multiplies matching entries; matrix product (@) does row-by-column dot products. Mixing them up gives wrong answers, sometimes silently.

manas.q: In NumPy, what is the difference between A * B and A @ B?

children.note: Comparing raw dot products favours long vectors. Normalise first, or use cosine similarity, when you only care about direction.
Modern AI turns words, images, songs or users into vectors called embeddings, so that "similar meaning" becomes "nearby in space".
An embedding is a learned list of numbers that represents an item. The model learns the numbers during training so that useful relationships show up as geometry.

manas.q: What is an embedding?

children.note: Good embeddings place "doctor" near "nurse" and "maize" near "wheat". Distance or cosine similarity then measures how related two items are.
A well-known word2vec example: the vector for king − man + woman lands near queen. Such neat patterns appear sometimes, not always, and should not be over-read.
A language model stores one row per token in an embedding matrix. Looking up a token simply means picking its row, which then flows through the network.

manas.q: How does a language model turn a token into a vector?

children.note: Real embeddings commonly have hundreds to a few thousand dimensions. More dimensions can hold finer distinctions but cost memory and compute.
To search by meaning, embed every document once, embed the question, and return the documents with the highest cosine similarity. Retrieval-augmented chatbots work this way.
A vector database stores millions of embeddings and finds nearest neighbours quickly, usually with approximate search methods that trade a little accuracy for speed.

children.topic: Limits: bias lives in the geometry
children.note: Embeddings learn from human text, so they can encode stereotypes, for example linking jobs to one gender. Measure and test them before trusting them.

manas.q: Why can embeddings be biased?

children.note: Eigenvectors reveal the directions a matrix treats specially. You will meet them in data compression, PCA and analysis of trained models.
An eigenvector v of matrix A keeps its direction when transformed: Av = λv. The number λ is the eigenvalue, the factor by which v is stretched or flipped.

manas.q: What equation defines an eigenvector v and eigenvalue λ of matrix A?

children.topic: Picture: the axes that do not turn
children.note: Most vectors get knocked off their line by a transformation. Eigenvectors stay on their own line, only getting longer, shorter or reversed.
Principal component analysis finds the eigenvectors of the data covariance matrix. The top ones point where the data varies most, so you can keep a few and drop the rest.

manas.q: What does PCA use eigenvectors for?

children.note: Singular value decomposition splits any matrix into rotation × stretch × rotation. It powers compression, recommender systems and noise removal.
A low-rank matrix can be written as the product of two thin matrices, using far fewer numbers. Fine-tuning methods such as LoRA train small low-rank updates instead of the full weight matrix.
Training and running AI is dominated by huge matrix multiplications. Graphics chips were built for exactly this kind of repetitive, parallel arithmetic.
Every entry of a matrix product can be computed separately from the others. That makes the work easy to split across thousands of small cores at once.

manas.q: Why is matrix multiplication well suited to GPUs?

children.note: A CPU has a few powerful cores good at varied, step-by-step tasks. A GPU has thousands of simpler cores that do the same operation on lots of data in parallel.
In large neural networks, most of the compute during training and use goes into matrix multiplications in the layers and attention.

manas.q: Which operation uses most of the compute in large neural networks?

children.note: Modern GPUs include units dedicated to small matrix multiplications, and Google built TPUs for the same job. Other chip makers offer similar accelerators.
Using 16-bit or 8-bit numbers instead of 32-bit lets chips do more multiplications per second and use less memory, usually with little loss in quality.
Moving numbers in and out of memory can take longer than the arithmetic itself. Good AI code keeps data on the GPU and reuses it.

nodeData.note: AI works with uncertain, noisy data and gives answers that are guesses with some chance of being wrong. Probability is the language for that uncertainty, and statistics is how we learn from data and judge how much to trust the result.

children.note: The core vocabulary: chances, events, random variables and how one event changes the chance of another.
0 means impossible, 1 means certain, 0.5 means as likely as not. Probabilities of all possible outcomes must add up to 1.

manas.q: What range must every probability fall in?

children.note: A classifier does not just say "malaria"; it gives, say, 0.82 for malaria and 0.18 for not. A language model gives a probability for every possible next token.
A random variable is a quantity whose value depends on chance, such as tomorrow's rainfall in Kisumu or the number of patients at a clinic today.
P(A | B) is the chance of A given that B is known to be true. P(rain | dark clouds) is higher than P(rain) on a random day.

manas.q: What does P(A | B) mean?

children.note: A and B are independent if knowing one tells you nothing about the other: P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B). Two fair coin flips are independent.

manas.q: When are two events independent?

children.note: The joint probability P(A, B) covers both happening together. Summing a joint table over one variable gives the marginal probability of the other.
A distribution describes all the values something can take and how likely each is. A few numbers like the mean and variance summarise it.
A probability distribution assigns chances to every possible outcome. It is the full picture; averages are just summaries of it.

manas.q: What is a probability distribution?

children.note: Discrete variables take separate values (number of children). Continuous ones take any value in a range (height). Continuous distributions use a density curve.
For continuous variables, probability is the area under the density curve over a range. A density value itself can be bigger than 1.
A handful of named distributions appear again and again in AI.
Bernoulli is one yes/no trial with chance p. Binomial counts the yeses in n independent trials, such as how many of 20 seeds sprout.
The bell curve, set by its mean and standard deviation. Many measurements are roughly normal, and it is used to initialise neural network weights.

manas.q: Which two numbers define a normal distribution?

children.note: Every value in a range is equally likely, like a fair die. Often used as a neutral starting assumption or for random initialisation.
One outcome out of k options, each with its own probability. A language model's next-token output is a categorical distribution over its vocabulary.

manas.q: What kind of distribution does a language model output for the next token?

children.note: Centre and spread are the two summaries you will use most.
The mean is the average: add the values and divide by how many there are. The expected value is the long-run average of a random variable.

manas.q: What is the expected value of a random variable?

children.note: The middle value when data is sorted. It resists outliers: one billionaire barely moves the median income but drags the mean up.
Variance is the average squared distance from the mean: Var = mean of (x − μ)². Standard deviation is its square root, in the same units as the data.

manas.q: How are variance and standard deviation related?

children.note: For a normal distribution about 68% of values lie within 1 standard deviation of the mean, 95% within 2 and 99.7% within 3.

manas.q: In a normal distribution, roughly what share of values lie within 2 standard deviations of the mean?

children.note: Bayes' rule tells you how to update a belief when new evidence arrives. It is the backbone of reasoning under uncertainty.
P(H | E) = P(E | H) × P(H) / P(E). It turns "how likely is the evidence if the hypothesis is true" into "how likely is the hypothesis now that I have seen the evidence".

manas.q: State Bayes' rule.

children.note: The prior P(H) is your belief before evidence. The likelihood P(E | H) is how well H explains the evidence. The posterior P(H | E) is your updated belief.

manas.q: What are the prior and the posterior in Bayes' rule?

children.note: A disease affects 1% of people. A test catches 90% of cases but wrongly flags 9% of healthy people. Of everyone testing positive, only about 9% actually have the disease.

manas.q: Why can a positive result from a fairly accurate test still mean a low chance of disease?

children.note: Ignoring how rare something is to begin with is a common reasoning error. A model screening for a rare condition will raise many false alarms unless this is accounted for.
A simple classifier that applies Bayes' rule while assuming features are independent given the class. Despite that crude assumption it works well for tasks like spam filtering.
Bayesian methods keep a whole distribution over model parameters instead of one best value, which gives a natural measure of uncertainty, at extra computing cost.
Most model training is a search for the parameters that make the observed data most probable.
Probability fixes the model and asks how likely different data are. Likelihood fixes the observed data and asks how well different parameter values explain it.

manas.q: What is the difference between probability and likelihood?

children.note: MLE picks the parameter values under which the observed data would be most likely. Many training methods are MLE in disguise.

manas.q: What does maximum likelihood estimation choose?

children.note: You see 7 heads in 10 flips. The likelihood of the data is highest when the coin's heads chance p = 0.7, so 0.7 is the maximum likelihood estimate.
Multiplying many small probabilities underflows to zero on a computer. Taking logs turns the product into a sum, which is stable and easier to optimise.
For classification and language models, the usual loss is the negative log of the probability given to the correct answer. Minimising it is the same as maximising likelihood.

manas.q: How is cross-entropy loss related to likelihood?

children.topic: Sampling: from data and from models
children.note: We learn from samples of the world, and generative models produce outputs by sampling. Both need care.
The population is everything you care about; a sample is the part you actually measured. Statistics is about saying something reliable about the population from the sample.

manas.q: What is the difference between a population and a sample?

children.note: If the sample is not representative, conclusions do not transfer. A skin-condition model trained mostly on light skin may fail on dark skin.
As a sample grows, its average gets closer to the true average. Small samples bounce around a lot.
Averages of many independent samples tend toward a normal distribution, whatever the original shape. This is why the bell curve shows up so often.

manas.q: What does the central limit theorem say?

children.note: Randomly split data so the model is judged on examples it never saw. The test set estimates how it will do on new data from the same source.
Chatbots sample the next token from a distribution. Low temperature sharpens it toward the top choice; high temperature flattens it for more variety and more mistakes.

manas.q: What does raising the sampling temperature do to a language model's output?

children.note: When exact maths is too hard, simulate many random samples and average the results. Used for estimating risk, integrals and uncertainty.
Knowing how strongly things move together is useful; knowing what causes what, and how sure you are, is harder.
Pearson correlation runs from −1 to 1. Near 1 means the two rise together, near −1 means one falls as the other rises, near 0 means no straight-line link.

manas.q: What range does the Pearson correlation coefficient take?

children.note: Two things moving together does not prove one causes the other. Ice-cream sales and drownings both rise in hot weather; heat drives both.

manas.q: Why does correlation not prove causation?

children.note: A confounder is a hidden third factor that affects both variables. Models trained on observational data happily learn confounded shortcuts.
Randomly assigning a treatment breaks the link with confounders, which is why randomised controlled trials are the strongest evidence of cause.
A 95% confidence interval comes from a method that captures the true value in about 95% of repeated samples. Narrow intervals need more data.

manas.q: What does a 95% confidence interval mean?

children.note: A p-value is how surprising the data would be if there were truly no effect. A small p-value is not the probability that the hypothesis is true.
A model is calibrated if, among predictions made with 80% confidence, about 80% are right. Many modern networks are overconfident, so check before trusting the numbers.

manas.q: What does it mean for a model to be well calibrated?

children.note: Clear visual explanations of the key ideas.

nodeData.note: Training an AI model means nudging millions of numbers so that its errors shrink. Calculus tells you which way to nudge each number, and optimisation is the step-by-step process of doing it.

children.note: A derivative tells you how fast one quantity changes when you change another a tiny bit. It is the basic tool behind all model training.
A model's error depends on its parameters. If you know how the error changes as each parameter moves, you know how to improve the model.
The derivative f'(x) is the slope of the curve at x: how much f changes per small step in x. Positive slope means going up, negative means going down.

manas.q: What does the derivative of a function tell you at a point?

children.note: f'(x) is the limit of (f(x + h) − f(x)) / h as the step h shrinks toward zero. It is the "instant" rate of change.
The derivative of f(x) = x² is 2x. At x = 3 the slope is 6, so a small step to the right raises f about 6 times as much as the step.

manas.q: What is the derivative of x², and its value at x = 3?

children.note: Power rule: xⁿ → n·xⁿ⁻¹. Constants drop out. The derivative of a sum is the sum of derivatives. With these you can handle most simple formulas.
At the bottom of a valley or top of a hill, the derivative is zero. Optimisation is largely a hunt for low points where the slope flattens.

manas.q: What is the derivative at the bottom of a smooth valley?

children.note: You can estimate a derivative numerically: (f(x + h) − f(x − h)) / 2h with a small h. Programmers use this to check that gradient code is correct.
Real models have millions of parameters. The gradient collects every slope into one vector.
A partial derivative measures change in one input while holding the others fixed, written ∂f/∂x. For f(x, y) = x² + 3y, ∂f/∂x = 2x and ∂f/∂y = 3.

manas.q: What is a partial derivative?

children.note: The gradient ∇f lists all partial derivatives: ∇f = [∂f/∂x1, …, ∂f/∂xn]. It has one entry per parameter.

manas.q: What is the gradient of a function?

children.note: The gradient points in the direction where the function rises fastest. Walking the opposite way is the fastest local way down.

manas.q: In which direction does the gradient point?

children.note: A large gradient means the surface is steep here; a tiny gradient means it is nearly flat, which can mean you are near a minimum or just stuck on a plateau.
Picture a hiking map with height lines. The gradient is always at right angles to the contour lines, pointing toward higher ground.
Neural networks are functions inside functions. The chain rule tells you how to get derivatives through every layer.
If y depends on u and u depends on x, then dy/dx = dy/du × du/dx. Rates of change multiply along the chain.

manas.q: State the chain rule.

children.note: For y = (3x + 1)², let u = 3x + 1. Then dy/du = 2u and du/dx = 3, so dy/dx = 6(3x + 1).
Backpropagation applies the chain rule from the loss back through each layer, reusing results so all gradients cost about as much as one extra forward pass.

manas.q: What is backpropagation?

children.note: Libraries like PyTorch and JAX record the operations you run and compute exact gradients for you. In PyTorch, loss.backward() fills in .grad for every parameter.

manas.q: What does loss.backward() do in PyTorch?

children.note: Multiplying many small factors through deep layers can shrink gradients to almost nothing, or many large ones can blow them up. Careful initialisation, normalisation and residual links help.

manas.q: What are vanishing gradients?

children.note: A loss function turns "how wrong is the model?" into one number that training tries to make small.
A loss maps the model's prediction and the true answer to a non-negative cost. Lower is better; zero means a perfect match.

manas.q: What is a loss function?

children.note: For predicting numbers: loss = average of (y − ŷ)². Squaring punishes big misses heavily, so outliers have a strong pull.

manas.q: What is the formula for mean squared error?

children.note: Loss = average of |y − ŷ|. It treats every unit of error the same, so it is less swayed by outliers than squared error.
For classification: loss = −log(probability the model gave the correct class). Confident wrong answers are punished very hard.

manas.q: Which loss is standard for classification and language models?

children.note: Accuracy is what people care about but it is not smooth, so it cannot guide gradients. We train on a smooth loss and report the metric separately.
Adding a penalty such as λ × (sum of squared weights) to the loss discourages over-complicated models and helps them generalise.
Gradient descent repeatedly steps against the gradient to lower the loss. Nearly every modern model is trained with a version of it.
w ← w − η × ∇L(w). Compute the gradient of the loss, take a small step the other way, repeat. η is the learning rate.

manas.q: Write the gradient descent update rule.

children.note: Imagine walking down a hill in thick fog. You cannot see the valley, but you can feel the slope under your feet and step downhill again and again.
Minimise L(w) = (w − 3)². The gradient is 2(w − 3). Start at w = 0 with η = 0.1: gradient −6, so w becomes 0.6, then about 1.08, creeping toward 3.
Full-batch uses all data per step, stochastic uses one example, mini-batch uses a small group. Mini-batches are the usual balance of speed and stability.

manas.q: What is mini-batch gradient descent?

children.note: One iteration is one update step. One epoch is one full pass over the training data, made of many mini-batch steps.
Momentum keeps a running average of past gradients to roll through small bumps. Adam also adapts the step size per parameter and is a common default.

manas.q: What does momentum add to plain gradient descent?

children.note: The learning rate is the step size, often the most important setting to tune.
Training is safe but painfully slow, and may stall before getting anywhere useful.
Steps overshoot the valley, so the loss bounces around or explodes to infinity or NaN.

manas.q: What happens if the learning rate is too large?

children.note: Many runs start with a short warm-up of small steps, then slowly decay the rate so training can settle into a good spot.
Try values like 0.1, 0.01, 0.001 and watch the loss curve. Good values differ between optimisers and models.
The loss surface of a big network is huge and bumpy. Knowing its features explains what can go wrong.
A global minimum is the lowest point anywhere; a local minimum is lowest only in its neighbourhood. Gradient descent can settle in a local one.

manas.q: What is the difference between a local and a global minimum?

children.note: A convex loss is bowl-shaped with only one minimum, so gradient descent will find it. Linear and logistic regression are convex; neural networks are not.

manas.q: Why is a convex loss easy to optimise?

children.note: A saddle point is flat in some directions and curves up in some and down in others. In high dimensions these and flat plateaus slow training more often than bad local minima.

manas.q: What is a saddle point?

children.note: In practice, very large networks usually reach low-loss regions that work well, and the noise from mini-batches helps escape poor spots. The full theory is still being studied.

children.topic: Low training loss is not the goal
children.note: A model can drive training loss near zero by memorising and still fail on new data (overfitting). Always watch validation loss too.
Steady fall is good; flat from the start suggests a bug or tiny learning rate; wild spikes suggest it is too high; widening train–validation gap suggests overfitting.
