nodeData.note: The transformer (2017) replaced step-by-step recurrent networks with self-attention, letting every token look at every other token in parallel. It now underlies nearly all large language models.

children.note: Language, audio and DNA come as ordered sequences where meaning depends on context, sometimes far back. Models must handle variable length and long-range links.
Text is split into tokens: words, word pieces or characters. Each token gets an id, and the model works on the sequence of ids.

manas.q: What is a token?

children.note: A common tokeniser: start from characters and repeatedly merge the most frequent pairs into new tokens. Common words become one token; rare words split into pieces.
Each token id is looked up in a learned table that returns a vector, for example 768 numbers. Similar tokens end up with similar vectors.
'Bank' means different things in 'river bank' and 'bank loan'. A good model must update each word's representation using its neighbours.
In 'The keys that the man left on the table are lost', the verb must agree with 'keys', several words back. Models need a way to connect distant positions.
Language models learn by predicting the next token from all previous ones. This simple objective, at large scale, teaches grammar, facts and patterns of reasoning.
Recurrent networks read a sequence one step at a time, carrying a hidden state forward like a running memory.
At each step: h_t = g(W·x_t + U·h_{t−1} + b). The same weights are reused at every step.

manas.q: How does an RNN process a sequence?

children.note: Backpropagating across many steps multiplies many small factors, so plain RNNs struggle to learn links more than a few dozen steps apart.
Long short-term memory, by Hochreiter and Schmidhuber, adds a cell state with input, forget and output gates that control what is kept. It holds information much longer.

manas.q: What are the three gates of an LSTM?

children.note: An encoder RNN compresses the source sentence into a vector; a decoder RNN writes the translation. One fixed vector became a bottleneck for long sentences.
Bahdanau and colleagues let the decoder look back at all encoder states and weight them. This attention idea is what transformers built on.
RNNs must compute step t before step t+1, so training cannot be parallelised across positions. This made very large models slow to train.

manas.q: Why are RNNs slow to train compared with transformers?

children.note: Self-attention lets every token look at every other token in the same sequence and pull in the information it needs.
Like searching a library, each token asks a question, compares it with every book's label, and reads a blend of the best matches instead of just one.
Each token's vector is multiplied by three learned matrices to get a query (what I seek), a key (what I offer) and a value (what I pass on).

manas.q: What are the query, key and value vectors in attention?

children.note: Compare a token's query with every key using a dot product. A high score means 'this token is relevant to me'.
Divide scores by √d_k so they do not grow too large, then apply softmax so each token's weights over all tokens add to 1.
Each token's new vector is the attention-weighted mix of all value vectors. Information flows directly between any two positions in one step.
Attention(Q, K, V) = softmax(Q·Kᵀ / √d_k) · V. This one line is the heart of the transformer.

manas.q: Write the scaled dot-product attention formula.

children.note: In a text generator, a token must not see future tokens. A mask sets those scores to −∞ before softmax, so their weights become 0.

manas.q: What does causal masking prevent?

children.note: Every token attends to every token, so compute and memory grow with n² for sequence length n. Long contexts are expensive, which drives much research.
A transformer stacks identical blocks; each mixes information across tokens, then processes each token separately.
Run several attention operations in parallel, each with its own Q, K, V matrices, then join the results. Different heads can track different relations.

manas.q: Why use multiple attention heads?

children.note: After attention, each token passes through the same small two-layer network (an MLP). Much of a model's stored knowledge is thought to sit here.
Each sub-layer adds its output back to its input (x + f(x)) and uses layer normalisation. This keeps very deep stacks trainable.
Attention alone ignores order, so position information is added. The 2017 paper used fixed sine and cosine waves; many models now use learned or rotary (RoPE) positions.

manas.q: Why do transformers need positional encoding?

children.note: The original model used 6 encoder and 6 decoder blocks. Today's large language models stack dozens of blocks with thousands of dimensions.
A final linear layer turns each position's vector into one score per vocabulary token; softmax gives the next-token probabilities.
The original transformer had an encoder and a decoder. Later models often keep only one half.
A paper by eight Google researchers introduced the transformer for machine translation, dropping recurrence entirely. It is among the most cited papers of the century.

manas.q: Which paper introduced the transformer, and when?

children.note: Reads the whole input with attention in both directions, producing a context-rich vector for each token. Good for understanding tasks.
Generates output one token at a time with causal masking. In the original design it also attends to the encoder's output (cross-attention).
Trained to fill in masked words using both sides of context. Used for classification, search and embeddings rather than free writing.

manas.q: What is an encoder-only model such as BERT good for?

children.note: Trained on next-token prediction and used for text generation. Most chat assistants (ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Llama) are built on this pattern.
Keeps both halves; natural for input-to-output tasks such as translation and summarisation.
Big transformers are first pre-trained on huge general data, then adapted with fine-tuning or instructions for specific uses.
The same blocks process image patches (ViT), audio frames and protein sequences, and multimodal models mix them.
Transformers parallelise well on GPUs, which made it practical to scale them to huge sizes.
Studies found that loss falls smoothly and predictably as parameters, data and compute grow together, following power laws. They are empirical patterns, not guarantees.

manas.q: What does a neural scaling law describe?

children.note: A 2022 DeepMind study (Chinchilla) found many large models were under-trained and that data should grow with model size, roughly 20 tokens per parameter.

manas.q: What did the Chinchilla study suggest about model size and data?

children.note: Some abilities seem to appear suddenly at scale. Researchers debate whether this is real or partly an effect of how skills are measured.
Generation picks the next token from the probabilities: greedy takes the top one; sampling with temperature, top-k or top-p adds variety.
Replaces one feed-forward layer with many 'expert' layers and a router that sends each token to only a few. Total parameters grow without every token paying for all of them.
Methods such as FlashAttention reorder the computation to save memory and time; others restrict which tokens attend to which to handle longer inputs.
When generating, keys and values of earlier tokens are stored and reused, so each new token does not recompute the whole past.
The maximum number of tokens the model can attend to at once. Longer windows cost more memory and the model may still miss details in the middle.
Transformers are powerful sequence models, but they have clear weaknesses.
A model trained to predict likely text can produce fluent but false statements. It has no built-in check against reality.

manas.q: Why do language models hallucinate?

children.note: Attention weights show where information flowed, but they are not a reliable account of why the model decided something.
Counting letters, arithmetic and some non-English languages suffer because tokens split text oddly. Many African and Indian languages need more tokens per word.
Training large transformers from scratch needs vast text and expensive hardware, so most people fine-tune or use existing models.
Common implementation errors: forgetting the causal mask, wrong head reshaping, and leaking future tokens during training, which gives falsely low loss.

nodeData.note: Large models are built in stages: pre-training on vast data with heavy compute, then fine-tuning and preference training, then compression and evaluation. This map explains each stage and its trade-offs.

children.note: A modern assistant model is made in stages: pre-training on huge general data, then fine-tuning and preference training, then compression and evaluation before release.
The model learns general patterns by predicting the next token over trillions of tokens. This is the most expensive stage by far.

manas.q: What does a language model learn during pre-training, and how?

children.note: Supervised fine-tuning on examples, then preference training (RLHF, RLAIF or similar) turns a raw text predictor into a helpful assistant.
A base model only continues text; asked a question, it might write more questions. The assistant version has been trained to follow instructions and refuse harmful ones.

manas.q: How does a base model differ from an assistant (chat) model?

children.note: Only a few well-funded labs pre-train frontier models. Most teams start from an existing open or licensed model and adapt it.
Open-weight models (for example Llama or Mistral releases) let you download and fine-tune the weights. Closed models are used through an API, sometimes with hosted fine-tuning.
Pre-training needs two scarce ingredients: huge amounts of good data and huge amounts of computation.
What goes in largely decides what comes out. Data work is a large share of the real effort.
Web crawls, books, code, scientific papers, encyclopedias and forum text, plus licensed and synthetic data. Exact mixes are often not disclosed.
Remove spam, boilerplate, toxic and low-quality text, and personal data where possible. Quality classifiers often score documents.
Repeated text wastes compute and raises the chance the model memorises and regurgitates it. Near-duplicate removal is standard.

manas.q: Why deduplicate pre-training data?

children.note: Web text is dominated by English. Swahili, Hindi and many other languages are under-represented, so models are weaker in them unless data is added deliberately.
Text generated by other models is increasingly used, especially for reasoning and code. Too much unchecked synthetic data can reduce diversity and quality.
Use of web and book text for training is debated and litigated in several countries. Check the current legal position where you work.
Training is mostly huge matrix multiplications, so it runs on GPUs or similar accelerators linked by fast networks.
GPUs run thousands of multiply-adds in parallel and have high memory bandwidth. Google's TPUs and other AI chips serve the same purpose.
A rough rule: training cost ≈ 6 × parameters × tokens floating-point operations. It lets you estimate cost before you start.

manas.q: What is the rough rule of thumb for training FLOPs?

children.note: Weights, gradients, optimiser states (Adam keeps two extra numbers per weight) and activations must fit in GPU memory.
Data parallel copies the model and splits batches; tensor parallel splits each layer; pipeline parallel splits the stack of layers across GPUs.

manas.q: Name three ways to split training across many GPUs.

children.note: Training with 16-bit numbers (bf16 or fp16) for most maths halves memory and speeds things up, while keeping sensitive parts in 32-bit.
Large training runs use a great deal of electricity and money. This concentrates frontier training in a few organisations and raises environmental questions.
Fine-tuning continues training a pre-trained model on a smaller, targeted dataset to change its behaviour or specialise it.
Knowledge from the general task is reused for a specific one, so far less data is needed than training from scratch.
Train on prompt-and-ideal-answer pairs, often thousands to tens of thousands. This teaches format, tone and instruction following.
Updates every weight. Most flexible, but needs memory for all gradients and optimiser states, and a full copy of the model per task.
PEFT methods freeze the original weights and train only a small number of new ones, such as adapters, prompts or LoRA matrices.
Low-rank adaptation adds a small update ΔW = B·A beside a frozen weight matrix, where A and B are thin matrices of rank r. Only A and B are trained.

manas.q: How does LoRA reduce the number of trainable parameters?

children.note: The change needed to adapt a model often lies in a low-dimensional space, so a rank of 8 or 16 can capture much of it.
Tiny adapter files per task, much less GPU memory, and the adapter can be merged into the weights so inference is not slower.
Keeps the frozen base model in 4-bit precision while training LoRA adapters, letting large models be fine-tuned on a single GPU.
Fine-tuning on a narrow task can erase earlier skills. Low learning rates, mixing in general data and PEFT methods reduce this.

manas.q: What is catastrophic forgetting?

children.note: Fine-tuning changes style and skills; retrieval (RAG) supplies fresh or private facts. For changing facts, RAG is usually cheaper and easier to update.
Preference training teaches a model which of several possible answers people, or written principles, judge better.
Reinforcement learning from human feedback: people rank model answers, a reward model learns to predict those rankings, then the model is optimised to score highly.

manas.q: What are the main steps of RLHF?

children.note: A network trained on human comparisons that outputs a score for a prompt and response. It stands in for a person during optimisation.
Proximal policy optimisation updates the model to raise reward while a penalty keeps it close to the original, so it does not drift into nonsense.
Reinforcement learning from AI feedback uses a model, guided by written principles, to produce the preference labels. Anthropic's Constitutional AI is one example.

manas.q: How does RLAIF differ from RLHF?

children.note: DPO trains directly on pairs of preferred and rejected answers without a separate reward model or reinforcement-learning loop. It is simpler to run.
The model may find ways to score well on the reward model without truly being better, such as being overly long or flattering.

manas.q: What is reward hacking?

children.note: Recent models are also trained with rewards on checkable tasks such as maths and code, encouraging longer step-by-step working before answering.
Before release, models are usually compressed to run cheaply and evaluated to check they are good and safe.
After training, models are often compressed so they are cheaper to run or fit on smaller devices.
A small student model is trained to match a large teacher's outputs, including its soft probabilities, not just the right answers.

manas.q: What is knowledge distillation?

children.note: The teacher's full probability list shows which wrong answers are close, which carries more information than a single correct label.
Store weights with fewer bits, for example 8-bit or 4-bit integers instead of 16-bit floats. Memory falls 2–4×, usually with a small accuracy cost.

manas.q: What does quantising a model do?

children.note: Post-training quantisation converts a finished model quickly. Quantisation-aware training simulates low precision during training for better accuracy.
Remove weights or whole parts that contribute little. Structured pruning removes entire heads or channels so hardware actually runs faster.
Quantised small models can run on a laptop or phone, which helps privacy and offline use, for example in clinics with poor internet.
Evaluation asks whether the model is actually good and safe for the intended use, not just whether its loss went down.
Perplexity is the exponential of average cross-entropy on unseen text; lower means the model predicts text better. It does not measure usefulness directly.

manas.q: What is perplexity, and is lower better?

children.note: Standard test sets such as MMLU (knowledge), HumanEval (code) and GSM8K (grade-school maths) let models be compared on the same questions.
If test questions leaked into training data, scores overstate ability. Fresh or private test sets help.

manas.q: What is benchmark contamination?

children.note: Once top models score near the maximum, a benchmark stops separating them, so the field keeps making harder ones.
Side-by-side human ratings, expert review and tests on your own real tasks often say more than public leaderboards.
Red-teaming and targeted tests check for harmful outputs, bias and misuse risk before and after release.
Training and adapting models goes wrong in predictable ways; knowing them saves time and money.
Fine-tuning on a few documents rarely makes a model recall them accurately and may increase confident errors. Use retrieval for facts.

manas.q: Is fine-tuning a reliable way to teach a model new facts?

children.topic: Bad data in, bad model out
children.note: A few hundred clean, consistent examples often beat thousands of messy ones. Review samples by hand before training.
Too many epochs on little data makes the model parrot its training answers. Watch validation loss and stop early.
Fine-tuning, even on harmless data, can weaken a model's refusal behaviour. Re-run safety tests after every fine-tune.
A bigger model may score slightly higher but cost far more per answer. Compare quality against speed, memory and price.
High public benchmark scores do not guarantee good results on your documents, language or users. Build a small test set of your own.

nodeData.note: Embeddings turn text and images into vectors so that similar meanings sit close together. This map covers similarity, vector databases, semantic and hybrid search, the retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) pipeline, how to evaluate it and common pitfalls.

children.note: An embedding is a list of numbers (a vector) that represents a word, sentence, image or document so that similar meanings sit close together.
A learned vector, often a few hundred to a few thousand numbers long. Distance between vectors stands in for difference in meaning.

manas.q: What is an embedding?

children.note: Early methods such as word2vec (2013) learned one vector per word from which words appear near each other. The famous example: king − man + woman ≈ queen.
word2vec gives 'bank' one vector everywhere. Transformer models give a different vector depending on the sentence, so 'river bank' and 'bank loan' differ.

manas.q: How do contextual embeddings differ from static word embeddings?

children.note: Models trained to embed whole passages so that a question and a passage answering it land close together. These power semantic search.
Often by contrastive learning: pull matching pairs (question and answer, image and caption) together, push random pairs apart.
Images, audio, code and products can be embedded too. Multimodal models put images and text in one shared space, so text can search photos.
Search with embeddings means finding the stored vectors closest to the query's vector.
cos = (a·b) / (|a|·|b|): the angle between two vectors, from −1 to 1. Higher means more similar, regardless of vector length.

manas.q: What does cosine similarity measure?

children.note: Dot product and Euclidean distance are alternatives. With normalised vectors (length 1), cosine and dot product rank results the same way.
More dimensions can hold finer meaning but cost more storage and search time. Some models let you shorten vectors with a small quality loss.

children.topic: Same model for query and documents
children.note: A query and documents must be embedded with the same model; vectors from different models are not comparable.

manas.q: Can you compare embeddings from two different embedding models?

children.note: A vector database stores embeddings and quickly finds the ones closest to a query, usually by approximate search. It can also filter results by metadata such as date or source.
Comparing the query with every one of millions of vectors is slow. Real systems use approximate nearest neighbour (ANN) search.
ANN trades a tiny chance of missing the true best match for search that is orders of magnitude faster.

manas.q: What trade-off does approximate nearest neighbour search make?

children.note: Common ANN approaches organise vectors for fast lookup.
Hierarchical navigable small-world graphs link each vector to near neighbours in layers, then hop toward the query. Fast and accurate, but memory-hungry.
Inverted-file indexes group vectors into clusters and only search the clusters nearest the query.
Compresses vectors into short codes so many more fit in memory, at some cost in accuracy.
Store fields like date, department or language with each vector, and filter on them, for example only search 2026 clinic guidelines.
Dedicated vector databases, vector extensions to ordinary databases such as Postgres, and libraries like FAISS. Pick by scale, cost and what you already run.
Semantic search matches meaning rather than exact words; hybrid search combines it with classic keyword search.
Classic ranking that scores documents by matching words, weighting rare words more. Excellent for names, codes and exact terms.

manas.q: What is keyword search like BM25 good at that embeddings may miss?

children.note: Finds 'fever in children' when the document says 'paediatric pyrexia'. Strong with paraphrases and synonyms, weaker on exact IDs and numbers.
Run both and merge the ranked lists, for example with reciprocal rank fusion. Often beats either one alone.

manas.q: Why combine keyword and semantic search?

children.note: A slower, more accurate model (a cross-encoder) re-scores the top 20–100 results by reading query and passage together, then keeps the best few.
Multilingual embedding models can match a Swahili question with an English document, but quality varies by language, so test with real queries.
Retrieval-augmented generation looks up relevant passages first, then gives them to a language model to answer from. The idea was proposed in 2020.
Models do not know private, recent or local documents and can make things up. RAG grounds answers in your sources without retraining the model.

manas.q: What two problems does RAG mainly address?

children.note: Collect and clean sources: PDFs, web pages, policies, notes. Extract text carefully, including tables, and keep titles and dates.
Split documents into passages small enough to retrieve precisely but large enough to make sense on their own.
Too small loses context; too large dilutes the match and wastes the prompt. A few hundred tokens with some overlap is a common start.

manas.q: What goes wrong if RAG chunks are too small or too large?

children.note: Split on headings, paragraphs or sections rather than fixed character counts, and attach the section title to each chunk.
Embed every chunk and store vector, text and metadata in the index. Re-embed when documents change.
Embed the user's question, fetch the top-k most similar chunks, optionally with hybrid search and reranking.
Put the retrieved chunks into the prompt with instructions: answer only from these sources, cite them, and say when the answer is not there.
The model writes the answer with references back to the chunks, so a person can check each claim.
Newer systems let the model decide what to search, run several queries, or read whole documents, at the cost of more time and complexity.
Measure retrieval and generation separately, so you know which half is failing.
Collect real questions with known correct answers and the source passages that contain them. Even 50–100 good cases help a lot.
Recall@k: did the right passage appear in the top k? MRR: how high did it rank? Poor retrieval caps the quality of every answer.

manas.q: What does recall@k measure in retrieval?

children.note: Is every claim in the answer supported by the retrieved text? An answer can be correct yet unsupported, or supported yet off-topic.

manas.q: What does faithfulness measure in a RAG answer?

children.note: Does the answer address the question, and does it match the reference answer? Expert review matters in high-stakes fields.
A language model can grade answers at scale, but its grades should be checked against human judgements on a sample.
Studies in medicine report that RAG can improve accuracy over a model alone, while warning that results vary and need careful clinical validation.
Most RAG failures come from data and retrieval, not from the language model.
Scanned PDFs with broken text, missing tables or duplicates lead to bad chunks and wrong answers. Inspect what was actually extracted.

manas.q: Where do most RAG failures usually start?

children.note: The top chunk may be similar in wording but outdated or about a different case. Use dates, filters and reranking.
With many chunks in a long prompt, models may overlook information placed in the middle. Retrieve fewer, better chunks.
RAG reduces but does not remove made-up answers; the model can mix in its own knowledge. Require citations and an 'I don't know' option.

manas.q: Does RAG eliminate hallucinations?

children.note: If documents change but embeddings are not refreshed, answers go out of date. Schedule re-indexing.
Users must only retrieve documents they are allowed to see. Patient or staff data needs protection under data laws such as Kenya's Data Protection Act; check the current text.
Retrieved text may contain instructions aimed at the model. Treat retrieved content as data, not as commands.

maps.title: Computer vision in practice: detection, OCR, medical images

nodeData.note: How vision models are put to work: detecting objects, outlining them, reading text and supporting doctors with medical images. Covers metrics, key model families, building and deploying a system, and where it fails. CNN basics are in the companion map.

children.note: Real projects start by choosing the right task. The same photo can be classified, boxed, outlined pixel by pixel, read as text or tracked over time, and each needs different labels and models.
One label for the whole image, such as 'healthy leaf' or 'diseased leaf'. Cheapest to label, but it cannot say where the thing is or how many there are.

manas.q: What can image classification not tell you?

children.note: Finds each object and draws a box around it with a class and a confidence score. Used for counting, locating and tracking things.

manas.q: What does an object detector output for each object?

children.note: Gives every pixel a class, such as road, sky or tumour, but does not separate two touching objects of the same class.
Like semantic segmentation, but each object gets its own mask, so two overlapping cells or cars are kept apart.

manas.q: How does instance segmentation differ from semantic segmentation?

children.note: Turns pictures of text into machine-readable characters, and in document AI also into structured fields like name, date and total.
Predicts keypoints such as elbows, knees and wrists, giving a stick-figure skeleton. Used in sports analysis, physiotherapy apps and gesture control.
Links detections across frames so each object keeps an ID over time. A common recipe is detect in every frame, then match boxes by position and appearance.

children.topic: Pick the simplest task that works
children.note: If a yes/no answer is enough, do not pay for pixel masks. Label cost rises steeply from class to box to mask.
A detector answers 'what is where'. It must handle many objects of different sizes, decide which guesses are duplicates, and be scored fairly.
Detection outputs are compared with human-drawn boxes using overlap, then summarised in a single score.
Usually stored as (x_min, y_min, x_max, y_max) or as centre, width and height, plus a class and a confidence between 0 and 1.
IoU = area of overlap ÷ area of union of two boxes. 1 means a perfect match, 0 means no overlap; 0.5 is a common cut-off for a correct hit.

manas.q: How is IoU calculated?

children.note: Non-maximum suppression keeps the highest-scoring box and deletes others of the same class that overlap it above an IoU threshold, then repeats.

manas.q: What problem does non-maximum suppression solve?

children.note: Precision: what share of predicted boxes were real objects. Recall: what share of real objects were found. Raising the confidence threshold trades recall for precision.
Average precision is the area under the precision–recall curve for one class; mAP averages it over classes. COCO-style mAP also averages over IoU thresholds from 0.5 to 0.95.

manas.q: What does mAP average over?

children.note: First propose regions that might contain objects, then classify and refine each one. Usually accurate, historically slower.
Ran a CNN on about two thousand cropped region proposals per image. Accurate for its time but very slow.
Fast R-CNN shared one CNN pass across all regions. Faster R-CNN added a learned Region Proposal Network, making the whole pipeline trainable.

manas.q: What did Faster R-CNN add to the R-CNN family?

children.note: Pre-set reference boxes of several sizes and shapes at each location. The network predicts small corrections to an anchor rather than a box from scratch.
Predict boxes and classes in a single forward pass over a grid, which makes real-time video detection practical.
'You Only Look Once', introduced by Joseph Redmon and colleagues. One network pass gives all boxes; many later versions from various groups improved speed and accuracy.

manas.q: Why is YOLO called 'You Only Look Once'?

children.note: Single Shot MultiBox Detector predicts boxes from feature maps at several scales, so small objects use fine maps and big objects use coarse ones.
One-stage models suit phones, drones and live cameras; two-stage models are still chosen when accuracy on small or crowded objects matters most.
DETR from Facebook AI treats detection as predicting a set of boxes with a transformer, matching them one-to-one to the ground truth. This removes anchors and NMS.

manas.q: Which hand-made steps does DETR remove?

children.note: Segmentation gives outlines rather than boxes, which matters when shape and area count: tumour size, field boundaries, road edges.
Combines both views: every pixel gets a class, and countable objects also get their own instance ID.
An encoder shrinks the image to capture context, a decoder grows it back, and skip connections pass fine detail across. Built for biomedical images and still a default there.

manas.q: What role do U-Net's skip connections play?

children.note: Adds a small mask-predicting branch to Faster R-CNN, so each detected box also gets a pixel mask. A standard instance segmentation baseline.
Dice = 2 × overlap ÷ (size of prediction + size of truth). Popular in medical segmentation; like IoU, 1 is perfect.

manas.q: What does the Dice score measure?

children.note: Meta's promptable model: click a point or draw a box and it returns a mask, even for object types it never saw labelled. Trained on over 1.1 billion masks.

manas.q: What makes Segment Anything 'promptable'?

children.note: SAM 2 (2024) extended prompting to video; SAM 3 (2025) added segmenting from short text concepts. Released under the Apache 2.0 licence.
Teams now often let SAM draft masks and have humans correct them, which is far faster than tracing outlines by hand.
Reading text from images is one of the most widely deployed vision uses: scanned forms, IDs, receipts, number plates and signs.

children.topic: Two steps: find text, read text
children.note: A text detector finds lines or words; a recogniser converts each crop into characters. Document AI then maps the text into fields.

manas.q: What are the two main stages of a modern OCR pipeline?

children.note: A CNN reads the crop as a strip of features and a sequence model outputs characters. CTC loss lets it learn without knowing exactly where each letter sits.
A free, open-source OCR engine first built at Hewlett-Packard in the 1980s, open-sourced in 2005 and sponsored by Google from 2006. Later versions added an LSTM recogniser.

manas.q: Where did the Tesseract OCR engine come from?

children.note: Printed pages on a flatbed are nearly solved. Curved, blurry, angled text on signs, labels or phone photos is much harder.
Handwriting recognition varies hugely by writer, language and script. Expect lower accuracy and plan for human checks on important fields.
Layout-aware models use both the words and their position on the page to pull out fields like total, date or ID number.
Modern multimodal models can read a photo of a document and answer questions about it. Handy, but they can invent text that is not there, so verify key values.

manas.q: What is the main risk when a vision-language model reads a document?

children.note: OCR is strongest for Latin script. Indian scripts like Devanagari or Tamil, and less-resourced languages, often need specific models and testing.
Vision models help read X-rays, scans, eye photos and slides. The best use today is assisting trained staff, with careful local testing.
Imaging gives lots of standardised pictures, which suits deep learning well.
Flags signs such as nodules, pneumothorax or tuberculosis patterns, and can sort normal from abnormal for faster reading.
3-D scans: models segment organs and tumours, measure volumes and prioritise urgent cases such as suspected brain bleeds.
A photo of the back of the eye can be graded for diabetic retinopathy, letting clinics without eye specialists screen many diabetics.
Whole-slide images can be billions of pixels. Models work on small tiles to find tumour regions or count cells.
CAD software highlights suspicious areas or scores an image to support a clinician's decision. It is a second opinion or a triage tool, not the final word.

manas.q: What is computer-aided detection meant to do?

children.note: Since 2021, WHO guidance has allowed CAD to read chest X-rays for TB screening and triage in people aged 15 and over. Positive results still need a lab test.

manas.q: For TB, what must follow a positive CAD result?

children.note: A 2024 Lancet Digital Health study tested 12 commercial TB CAD products on 774 people. Accuracy and best thresholds differed by product, version and group; all did worst in older people, people with HIV and those with past TB.

manas.q: Why must a TB CAD threshold be chosen locally?

children.topic: 📄 Eye screening AI in Punjab, India
children.note: A 2026 study compared three commercial diabetic retinopathy AIs on two fundus cameras in a primary health centre. Sensitivity and specificity shifted with the camera.
Clinical AI is a medical device: the FDA in the US, CE marking in Europe and national regulators elsewhere must clear it for a stated use. Radiology has the most cleared AI tools.
In 2018 the US FDA authorised IDx-DR to screen for diabetic retinopathy without a specialist reading the image. It is limited to a defined patient group and camera.
A model trained on one hospital's scanners, population and protocols can lose accuracy elsewhere. New camera, new disease mix or new age group all count.

manas.q: Name three causes of dataset shift in medical imaging.

children.note: Models miss rare findings, cannot see the patient's history, and fail silently on unusual images. Clinicians stay accountable and catch these errors.
Documented deployments show both the promise and the gap between lab scores and field results.
Researchers used transfer learning on field photos of cassava leaves from Tanzania to recognise three diseases and two kinds of pest damage, reaching 93% on held-out images.

manas.q: Which technique let a small cassava photo dataset train an accurate model?

children.note: A 2019 follow-up put a cassava detector in a mobile app. On real field photos its F1 score fell by about a third, mostly from missed cases.
CAD chest X-ray reading is used in TB case-finding where radiologists are scarce, including in African and South Asian programmes.
Cameras spot defects on production lines, check shelves for missing stock and read barcodes. Fixed lighting and angles make these among the most reliable uses.
Automatic number-plate recognition combines detection and OCR for tolls, parking and enforcement, which also raises privacy questions.
Banks, telecoms and governments use OCR to read ID cards and forms during sign-up and checks. Errors and fraud attempts mean human review remains part of the flow.
Most practical vision systems are built by fine-tuning a pretrained model on a few hundred to a few thousand well-labelled local images.
Write down the task type, classes, metric and target, for example 'recall above 95% on blurry phone photos'. This decides labels and model.
Draw boxes, masks or text transcripts with an annotation tool. Write a labelling guide with examples, since vague rules give noisy labels.

manas.q: Why write a labelling guide before annotating?

children.note: Have two people label a sample and compare. Disagreement shows unclear classes; in medicine, use expert readers or lab-confirmed outcomes.
Start from a model pretrained on large datasets like COCO and retrain the final layers on your data. Far less data and compute than training from scratch.

manas.q: Why fine-tune a pretrained detector instead of training from scratch?

children.note: In torchvision: m = fasterrcnn_resnet50_fpn(weights='DEFAULT'); then m.roi_heads.box_predictor = FastRCNNPredictor(1024, num_classes). Train only on your images.
Add flips, crops, brightness, blur and rotation that mimic real conditions. For detection, transform the boxes together with the image.
Keep all images of one patient, field or camera in a single split. Otherwise near-duplicates leak into testing and scores look too good.

manas.q: Why split medical images by patient rather than by image?

children.note: Phones, cameras and drones need small, fast models. Quantisation (e.g. 8-bit weights), pruning and compact architectures cut size and delay, usually with slight accuracy loss.

manas.q: What does quantisation do to a model for edge devices?

children.topic: Test where it will be used
children.note: Collect a fresh test set from the real users, devices and lighting. Lab accuracy often drops in the field, as the cassava app showed.
Log confidence scores and sample predictions for human review. Retrain when cameras, seasons or populations change.
Vision models are powerful pattern matchers but not robust seers. Know where they break before trusting them.
If training images under-represent darker skin, women, older people or rural settings, accuracy drops for those groups. Report results per subgroup.

manas.q: How do you detect bias in a vision model?

children.note: Tiny, carefully designed changes to pixels or a printed sticker can make a detector miss a person or misread a sign, while humans see no difference.
Models can latch onto hospital markers, rulers or backgrounds instead of the disease or object. Heatmaps and outside-site testing help reveal this.
A high score is not a probability of being right, especially on unusual images. Calibrate scores and send low-confidence or odd cases to a person.
Face recognition and number-plate cameras can track people at scale. Many laws, such as the EU AI Act, restrict some uses; check the current text.
Medical images and IDs are personal data. In Kenya the Data Protection Act applies; get consent, minimise data and secure storage.
Videos found today that show detection, segmentation, OCR and medical imaging at work.
YOLO's creator Joseph Redmon demonstrates real-time detection and explains why it should be open and fast.
Stanford lecture covering R-CNN, YOLO-style detectors, segmentation and how to visualise what networks learn.
A walk-through of how OCR turns images of text into characters and why it can go wrong.
A clear explainer from JAMA Network on how models are trained and evaluated on medical images.
Shows adversarial examples: small image changes that fool a classifier.

nodeData.note: Python is the main language people use to build, train and test AI. It is easy to read, free, and connects to fast libraries for data and deep learning, so learning it opens nearly every AI tool and course.

children.note: Python won the AI world through readability and a huge set of libraries, not raw speed.
Python code reads close to plain English and uses indentation instead of braces. You can focus on the idea rather than the syntax.

manas.q: Why is Python considered beginner-friendly?

children.note: Heavy maths in NumPy and PyTorch runs in compiled C, C++ or CUDA code. Python just orchestrates it, so it is fast where it counts.

manas.q: How can Python be slow yet still run AI fast?

children.note: Almost every AI library, tutorial, research code release and course offers Python first. That network effect keeps it on top.
Python is open source and runs on Windows, Mac, Linux, Raspberry Pi and in the browser through tools like Colab.
Plain Python loops are slow, and mobile or web apps often use other languages. For data and model work these rarely matter.
C++ and CUDA for speed, R for statistics, JavaScript for web apps, Julia for scientific computing, Rust for tooling. Python remains the common ground.
The small core of the language you need before touching AI libraries.
x = 5 stores an int, y = 2.5 a float, name = "Amina" a string, ok = True a boolean. Python works out the type for you.
A list is an ordered collection: [3, 1, 4]. A dictionary maps keys to values: {"crop": "maize", "yield": 2.1}. Most data starts in one of these.

manas.q: What is the difference between a list and a dictionary in Python?

children.note: if chooses between paths, for loops over items, while repeats until a condition fails. These three control almost every program.
Python uses indentation (usually 4 spaces) to mark which lines belong to a loop or function. Wrong indentation is an error, not just bad style.

manas.q: What does indentation do in Python?

children.note: def area(r): return 3.14 * r * r defines a reusable block. Good functions do one job and have clear names.

manas.q: Which keyword defines a function in Python?

children.note: import math or import numpy as np brings in code others wrote. Most AI work is importing the right library and calling it well.
squares = [x * x for x in range(10)] builds a list in one readable line. You will see this pattern everywhere.
A traceback shows where things went wrong; read the last line first. Pasting the error into a search or an assistant is normal practice.
Most AI learning and experimenting happens in notebooks that mix code, results, charts and notes.
A notebook is a document of cells: code cells you run one at a time and text cells for explanation. Outputs and plots appear right below the code.

manas.q: What is a notebook in data science?

children.note: Project Jupyter is the open-source notebook system, spun off from IPython in 2014. Its .ipynb files are the standard notebook format.

manas.q: Which open-source project created the standard notebook format?

children.note: Colab runs Jupyter-style notebooks in the browser with nothing to install and offers limited free GPU time. Good for learning when your laptop is weak.

manas.q: What does Google Colab give a beginner?

children.note: Kaggle notebooks offer free compute and datasets; VS Code and JupyterLab run notebooks locally on your own machine.
Cells can be run in any order, so the notebook state may not match what you see. Use "Restart and run all" before trusting or sharing results.

manas.q: Why should you "restart and run all" before sharing a notebook?

children.note: Once code is reused or runs for hours, move it into .py files and modules. Scripts are easier to test, version and run on servers.
You do not need every library. Know which one does which job.
Libraries for numbers, tables and charts.
NumPy provides n-dimensional arrays and fast vectorised maths. It is the foundation most other scientific libraries build on.

manas.q: What does NumPy provide?

children.note: pandas gives the DataFrame, a spreadsheet-like table for loading CSVs, cleaning, filtering and grouping data.

manas.q: What is the main data structure in pandas?

children.note: Matplotlib draws almost any plot; seaborn adds attractive statistical charts with less code. Always plot your data before modelling.
For tables of data, these often beat deep learning.
scikit-learn offers regression, classification, clustering, and evaluation tools behind one simple pattern: model.fit(X, y) then model.predict(X_new).

manas.q: What two methods sit at the heart of the scikit-learn API?

children.note: XGBoost, LightGBM and CatBoost build strong models from many small decision trees and are frequent winners on tabular data.
Frameworks for building and training neural networks on GPUs.
PyTorch offers tensors on GPU plus automatic gradients. Originally built at Meta and now under the Linux Foundation, it is widely used in research and industry.

manas.q: What two core features does PyTorch provide?

children.note: TensorFlow and JAX come from Google; Keras is a high-level API for building models quickly. JAX is popular for large-scale research.
Using ready-made models instead of training from scratch.
The transformers and datasets libraries let you download and run thousands of pretrained open models in a few lines.
Providers such as Anthropic, OpenAI and Google offer Python SDKs to call their hosted models. Keep API keys out of your code and notebooks.
A clean setup avoids most "it works on my machine" headaches.
Get Python 3 from python.org or your system's package manager. Python 2 is long retired; ignore old tutorials that use it.
A virtual environment is a separate folder of packages per project, so versions do not clash. Create one with python -m venv .venv, then activate it.

manas.q: Why use a virtual environment for each project?

children.note: pip install numpy pandas downloads packages from PyPI into the active environment.

manas.q: Which tool installs Python packages from PyPI?

children.note: pip freeze > requirements.txt saves exact versions so others, or future you, can rebuild the same setup.

manas.q: What is requirements.txt for?

children.note: conda manages Python plus non-Python libraries, popular in data science. Newer tools such as uv install packages much faster. Pick one approach and stick to it.
Deep learning on an NVIDIA GPU needs a matching driver and a PyTorch build for your CUDA version. The PyTorch website gives the right install command.
An editor like VS Code helps with autocomplete and debugging. Git tracks changes so you can undo mistakes and share code.
A practical order to go from zero to building AI projects. Move on when you can do each step without copying.
Variables, lists, dictionaries, loops, functions and files. Write small programs, such as a budget tracker or a quiz.

children.topic: 2. NumPy and pandas on real data
children.note: Load a real dataset, for example rainfall, crop prices or clinic visits, then clean, summarise and plot it.
Train and evaluate simple models: split data, fit, measure accuracy, try another model and compare.
Build a small network, write a training loop, and watch the loss fall. Then use a pretrained model.
Call a model API or a Hugging Face model, add retrieval over your own documents, and wrap it in a simple app.
Assistants speed you up, but read and test every line they write. If you cannot explain the code, you have not learned it yet.

manas.q: What is the main rule for learning with AI coding assistants?

children.note: Habits that waste beginners' time.
Looping over a million numbers in plain Python is slow. Use NumPy or pandas operations that work on whole arrays at once.

manas.q: Why prefer vectorised NumPy operations over Python loops?

children.note: Watching course after course without building anything feels productive but sticks poorly. Build a small project after each topic.
Code from an old tutorial may break with new library versions. Check versions and read the current documentation.

maps.title: Working with data: NumPy and pandas

nodeData.topic: Working with data: NumPy and pandas
nodeData.note: Hands-on guide to the Python tools used before and around every AI project: NumPy arrays, pandas tables, cleaning, grouping, plotting, and a first scikit-learn model.

children.note: Before any model is trained, data has to be loaded, checked and reshaped. In Python, that everyday work is done mostly with NumPy, pandas, Matplotlib and scikit-learn.
NumPy gives fast arrays, pandas gives labelled tables on top of NumPy, Matplotlib draws charts, and scikit-learn trains classic machine-learning models. They are free and open source.

manas.q: Which library does pandas build on?

children.note: Most people start in a notebook (Jupyter, or a hosted one such as Google Colab) where code, output and charts sit together. Scripts in a code editor are better once the work must be repeated.
In real projects, finding, cleaning and understanding the data usually takes far longer than training the model. Good data work is the main skill, not a side task.
Think of a CSV of clinic visits in Nairobi: date, age, county, diagnosis, cost. We will load it, clean it, summarise it, plot it and finally predict something from it.
NumPy adds the ndarray: a grid of numbers of one type, stored compactly so maths on whole arrays runs in fast compiled code instead of slow Python loops.
An n-dimensional array of same-type values, for example a vector (1-D), a table of numbers (2-D) or a batch of images (4-D). Every array has a shape and a dtype.

manas.q: What two properties describe every NumPy array?

children.note: Shape is the size along each axis, e.g. (100, 3) for 100 rows and 3 columns. Dtype is the number type, such as int64 or float32; float32 halves memory compared with float64.
Write a * 2 + b instead of a loop and NumPy applies it to every element at once. This is often tens to hundreds of times faster than plain Python loops.

manas.q: Why is vectorised NumPy code faster than a Python loop?

children.note: NumPy stretches a smaller array to match a bigger one when shapes are compatible, so you can subtract a per-column mean (shape (3,)) from a (100, 3) table in one line.

manas.q: What does broadcasting let you do?

children.note: a[0] is the first row, a[:, 1] the second column, and a[a > 0] keeps only positive values (boolean masking). Slices usually return views that share memory, so edits can affect the original.
np.mean, np.sum, np.std with an axis argument summarise along rows or columns; np.reshape changes shape; a @ b does matrix multiplication; np.random makes random data for tests.
NumPy was created in 2005 by Travis Oliphant, merging the earlier Numeric and Numarray libraries. Its design is described in the 2020 Nature paper "Array programming with NumPy".
pandas adds labelled tables (DataFrames) and columns (Series), making spreadsheet-style work scriptable and repeatable. Wes McKinney began it around 2008.
A Series is one labelled column of values; a DataFrame is a table of Series sharing a row index. Each column has its own dtype, so text, dates and numbers can sit side by side.

manas.q: What is the difference between a Series and a DataFrame?

children.note: df = pd.read_csv("visits.csv") reads a file into a DataFrame. Options like parse_dates, sep and encoding handle dates, semicolon files and non-English characters.
df.head() shows the first rows, df.info() shows columns, dtypes and missing counts, and df.describe() gives count, mean, spread and quartiles for numeric columns.

manas.q: Which three commands give a quick first look at a DataFrame?

children.note: df["age"] picks a column; df.loc uses labels, df.iloc uses positions. df[df.age > 60] filters rows with a condition, just like NumPy masking.

manas.q: What is the difference between .loc and .iloc?

children.note: Assign directly: df["cost_usd"] = df.cost_kes / 130 (use a real exchange rate). Operations act on the whole column at once, like NumPy.
pandas also reads Excel, JSON, Parquet and SQL databases. Parquet is compact and keeps dtypes, so it is a good format for saving cleaned data.
Real data has gaps, typos, duplicates and wrong types. Cleaning makes it trustworthy before any analysis or model sees it.
df.isna().sum() counts gaps per column. You can drop rows (dropna) or fill gaps (fillna) with a sensible value, but always ask why data is missing first.

manas.q: How do you count missing values per column in pandas?

children.note: Numbers read as text break maths. pd.to_numeric and pd.to_datetime convert columns; errors="coerce" turns bad entries into missing values you can inspect.
"Nairobi", "nairobi " and "NBI" may mean the same county. Use .str.strip().str.lower() and a mapping table to standardise labels.
df.duplicated() flags repeated rows and drop_duplicates() removes them. Decide which columns define a true duplicate, e.g. patient ID plus visit date.
An age of 250 or a negative cost is an error, not an insight. Check ranges with describe() and plots, and fix or remove with a written reason.
Never overwrite the original file. Write cleaning as code from raw to clean so anyone can rerun it and see every change.

manas.q: Why should cleaning steps be written as code rather than done by hand?

children.note: Most questions are "per something": cost per county, visits per month. pandas answers them with group-by, pivot tables and joins.
groupby splits rows into groups, applies a function to each, and combines results: df.groupby("county")["cost"].mean() gives average cost per county.

manas.q: What three steps does groupby perform?

children.note: .agg(["mean", "median", "count"]) returns many statistics in one table. Median is safer than mean when a few huge values distort the average.
df["diagnosis"].value_counts() lists how often each category appears, a quick way to spot rare classes and typos.
pd.pivot_table turns long data into a grid, e.g. counties as rows, months as columns, visit counts as cells, much like a spreadsheet pivot.
pd.merge combines tables on a shared key, like adding county population to visit data. Check row counts after merging to catch missing or duplicated matches.
With a datetime column you can resample("ME") (month end) to get monthly totals or use rolling(7).mean() for a 7-day moving average.
A chart often reveals errors and patterns that tables hide. Matplotlib is the base library; pandas and seaborn call it underneath.
Create a figure and axes, draw on the axes, add labels and a title, then show or save. plt.plot, plt.bar, plt.hist and plt.scatter cover most needs.
df["age"].plot(kind="hist") or df.plot(x="date", y="visits") makes a quick chart with sensible defaults.
Line for change over time, bar for comparing groups, histogram for one variable's distribution, scatter for the relationship between two numbers.

manas.q: Which chart shows the distribution of a single numeric variable?

children.note: Every chart needs axis labels with units and a clear title. Start bar charts at zero so differences are not exaggerated.
seaborn builds on Matplotlib to make grouped and statistical plots, such as box plots per category, with less code.
scikit-learn offers many classic algorithms behind one consistent interface, which makes it the usual first step into machine learning in Python.
X holds the input columns (features) and y the column to predict (target). For example, predict whether a visit leads to admission from age, county and symptoms.

manas.q: In scikit-learn, what do X and y usually hold?

children.note: train_test_split keeps some rows hidden from training so you can measure performance on unseen data. Testing on training data gives falsely good scores.

manas.q: Why hold back a test set?

children.note: Every estimator follows the same pattern: model = LogisticRegression(); model.fit(X_train, y_train); model.predict(X_test). Swapping algorithms changes only the first line.
Models need numbers. One-hot encoding turns a county column into 0/1 columns; scaling puts features on similar ranges for models that care about scale.
A Pipeline chains preprocessing and the model so the exact same steps run on training and new data, preventing information from the test set leaking in.

manas.q: What problem does a scikit-learn Pipeline help prevent?

children.note: Accuracy is the share of correct predictions, but with rare classes look at precision, recall and the confusion matrix. For numbers, use error measures like mean absolute error.
Instead of one split, k-fold cross-validation trains and tests k times on different folds and averages the scores, giving a steadier estimate.
Compare against a trivial model, such as always predicting the most common class. If your model barely beats it, it has not learned much.
Most errors in data work are quiet: the code runs but the answer is wrong. Knowing the usual traps saves weeks.
Changing a filtered slice may not change the original DataFrame. Use .loc for assignments or make an explicit .copy() when you want a separate table.
Using information at training time that would not exist at prediction time, such as a column filled in after the outcome, gives great scores that collapse in real use.

manas.q: What is data leakage?

children.note: Data from one city hospital may not represent rural patients. A model is only as fair and general as the data it learned from.
Health and personal records need permission and protection. Remove names and IDs you do not need, and follow your country's data law, e.g. Kenya's Data Protection Act; check the current text.
A grouped summary or a model can show that two things move together, not that one causes the other.
Hands-on video courses that walk through the same tools with real datasets.
freeCodeCamp hour-long walk through creating, indexing and computing with NumPy arrays.
freeCodeCamp course covering NumPy, pandas, Matplotlib and seaborn on real datasets.
Corey Schafer builds and customises line plots step by step.
freeCodeCamp introduction to models, pipelines and evaluation in scikit-learn.
Short, clear explanation of why and how to cross-validate a model.
Free documentation and articles for going deeper.
History and design of the pandas library.
The 2020 Nature paper by the NumPy developers describing how and why it works.
Documentation, user guide and getting-started tutorials.
The official guide to every model, preprocessing step and metric.
The official Python tutorial, for filling gaps in the core language.

nodeData.note: A hands-on route through PyTorch: tensors, automatic gradients, building networks with nn.Module, the training loop, GPUs, saving models, and using pretrained models from Hugging Face.

children.note: PyTorch is an open-source deep-learning library for Python. It began at Meta (Facebook) and is now developed with support from the Linux Foundation; it is widely used in research and industry.
PyTorch grew out of Torch, an older library written for the Lua language, and brought the same ideas to Python.
PyTorch builds the computation graph as your Python code runs, so you can use ordinary loops, ifs and print statements and debug like normal Python.

manas.q: What does "define-by-run" mean in PyTorch?

children.note: Tensors hold the numbers, autograd computes gradients, and torch.nn provides building blocks for networks. Everything else is built from these.
TensorFlow/Keras and JAX solve the same problem. The ideas below (tensors, gradients, training loops) carry across all of them.
A tensor is PyTorch's array: like a NumPy ndarray, but it can live on a GPU and track gradients.
torch.tensor([1., 2.]), torch.zeros(3, 4), torch.randn(2, 3) for random normal values. torch.from_numpy shares memory with a NumPy array.
Every tensor has a shape (e.g. [32, 3, 224, 224] for 32 colour images), a dtype (float32 by default) and a device (cpu or cuda).

manas.q: What three attributes should you check on a tensor when debugging?

children.note: Elementwise maths, matrix multiply (a @ b), reshaping with view/reshape and broadcasting work much as in NumPy.
By convention the first dimension is the batch: many examples processed together. Shape mismatches are the most common beginner error.

manas.q: By convention, what does the first dimension of a tensor usually hold?

children.note: Images become [batch, channels, height, width]; text becomes integer token IDs [batch, sequence]; tables become [batch, features].
Autograd is PyTorch's automatic differentiation engine. It records operations on tensors and uses the chain rule to compute gradients for you.
Tensors created with requires_grad=True are tracked. Model parameters have it switched on automatically.
During the forward pass PyTorch records each operation in a graph. Calling loss.backward() walks the graph in reverse to find each gradient.

manas.q: What does loss.backward() do?

children.note: After backward(), each parameter's .grad holds d(loss)/d(parameter): how the loss changes if that weight is nudged.
Each backward() adds to .grad rather than replacing it, so you must clear gradients every step with optimizer.zero_grad().

manas.q: Why must you call optimizer.zero_grad() each step?

children.note: Wrap evaluation in torch.no_grad() (or torch.inference_mode()) to save memory and time when you do not need gradients.
x = torch.tensor(3., requires_grad=True); y = x**2; y.backward() then x.grad is 6, because dy/dx = 2x.
Networks are Python classes that subclass nn.Module: layers are created in __init__ and used in forward().
nn.Linear (fully connected), nn.Conv2d (images), nn.Embedding (tokens), nn.LayerNorm and nn.Dropout are common building blocks.
Non-linear functions such as ReLU or GELU between layers let a network learn more than straight-line relationships.

manas.q: Why are activation functions needed between layers?

children.note: forward(x) says how input flows through layers to produce output. You call model(x), not model.forward(x), so PyTorch hooks run correctly.
For a simple stack of layers, nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(4, 16), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(16, 3)) avoids writing a class.
model.parameters() yields every learnable tensor; the optimizer is given this list. Counting them tells you the model's size.
nn.CrossEntropyLoss for classification, nn.MSELoss for regression (loss = mean of (y − ŷ)²). CrossEntropyLoss expects raw scores (logits), not softmax output.

manas.q: Should you apply softmax before nn.CrossEntropyLoss?

children.note: Unlike some libraries, PyTorch makes you write the loop yourself. It is the same five steps every time.
A Dataset returns one example by index; a DataLoader groups examples into shuffled batches and can load them in parallel.

manas.q: What does a DataLoader add on top of a Dataset?

children.note: For each batch: predict (forward), compute loss, zero old gradients, backward() to get new gradients, optimizer.step() to update weights.

manas.q: Name the five steps of a PyTorch training step.

children.note: torch.optim.SGD and torch.optim.AdamW update weights using gradients. The learning rate sets the step size and is the most important setting to tune.
One epoch is one full pass over the training data. Training usually runs many epochs while watching validation loss.
model.train() turns on dropout and batch-norm updates; model.eval() turns them off for validation and use. Forgetting this gives odd results.

manas.q: What changes when you call model.eval()?

children.note: If training loss keeps falling but validation loss rises, the model is memorising. Stop early, add data, regularise or simplify.
GPUs run thousands of simple maths operations in parallel, which can make training many times faster than on a CPU.
device = "cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu". Apple-silicon Macs can use "mps".
Call model.to(device) once and move each batch with x.to(device). Every tensor in one operation must be on the same device, or PyTorch raises an error.

manas.q: What must be true of all tensors in one PyTorch operation?

children.note: Hosted notebooks such as Google Colab or Kaggle offer limited free GPU time, enough for learning projects.
torch.autocast runs parts of the model in 16-bit numbers, saving memory and speeding up training on modern GPUs with little loss of accuracy.
CUDA out of memory usually means the batch or model is too big. Reduce batch size, use mixed precision, or accumulate gradients over smaller batches.
Trained weights are valuable; save them so you can resume training or use the model later without retraining.
torch.save(model.state_dict(), "model.pt") stores the weights as a dictionary of tensors. This is the recommended way.

manas.q: What is the recommended thing to save in PyTorch: the whole model or its state_dict?

children.note: Recreate the model class, then model.load_state_dict(torch.load("model.pt")). The architecture code must match the saved weights.
For long training, also save the optimizer state and epoch number so you can resume exactly where you stopped.
torch.load uses Python pickling, which can run code. Newer versions default to weights_only=True; still load only trusted files. safetensors is a safer format.
The Transformers library from Hugging Face gives ready access to thousands of pretrained models, mostly run on PyTorch, through a few lines of code.
Hugging Face hosts a public hub of models, datasets and demo apps. Each model page has a card describing its training, licence and limits.
pipeline("sentiment-analysis") downloads a default model and its tokenizer and returns predictions. Good for trying a task quickly.

manas.q: What does the Transformers pipeline() function do?

children.note: For control, load AutoTokenizer and AutoModel with the same model name. The tokenizer turns text into the token IDs the model expects.
Start from a pretrained model and train a little more on your own labelled data, e.g. Swahili customer messages. This needs far less data and compute than training from scratch.

manas.q: Why fine-tune instead of training from scratch?

children.note: Check each model's licence before commercial use, and read its card for known biases and languages covered.
Deep-learning bugs often give no error, just a model that learns badly.
If your model cannot drive the loss near zero on a single small batch, there is a bug. This quick test catches most wiring mistakes.

manas.q: What simple test checks that a training loop is wired correctly?

children.topic: Learning rate too high or low
children.note: Too high and the loss jumps or becomes NaN; too low and it barely moves. Try values spread by factors of 10.
Inputs on very different scales slow or break training. Normalise features and image pixels.
Set torch.manual_seed for repeatable runs, and report results over several seeds, since one run can be lucky.
Video courses from first tensors to building networks by hand.
Very short overview of what PyTorch is and why it is popular.
Long hands-on course from tensors to computer-vision projects.
Andrej Karpathy writes a tiny autograd engine to show exactly how backpropagation works.
Visual explanation of how gradients flow back through a network.
Official Hugging Face course video on using pipeline().
Official tutorials and free courses.
Official step-by-step tutorials, from basics to advanced topics.
History and design of the library, including autograd.
Free courses on Transformers, fine-tuning and more.
Free interactive textbook with runnable PyTorch code.
Practical deep-learning course built on PyTorch.

nodeData.note: How to build software on top of large language models: keeping keys safe, messages and system prompts, settings, tokens and cost, tool use, structured output, evaluation, and running open-weight models locally.

children.note: An LLM API lets your own program send text to a large language model hosted by a provider and get text back, so you can build apps without training a model.
Your code sends an HTTPS request with the model name, messages and settings; the provider returns the generated text plus usage information.

manas.q: What does a typical LLM API request contain?

children.note: Providers publish client libraries (SDKs) for Python, JavaScript and other languages that wrap the raw HTTP calls.
Anthropic (Claude), OpenAI (GPT models), Google (Gemini) and others offer APIs; open-weight models can also be served through compatible APIs.
The model does not remember earlier calls. To continue a conversation you send the earlier messages again each time.

manas.q: Does an LLM API remember previous requests?

children.note: An API key is like a password tied to your account and bill. Leaking it lets others spend your money.
Store the key in an environment variable or a secrets manager, and have code read it from there instead of writing it in the source.

manas.q: Where should an API key be stored instead of in code?

children.note: Add .env files to .gitignore. Keys pushed to a public repository are often found and abused within minutes; if it happens, revoke the key at once.
Never put a key in a mobile app or browser JavaScript, where anyone can extract it. Route calls through your own server.
Set spending limits and usage alerts in the provider console, and use separate keys per project so one can be revoked alone.
Text you send goes to the provider. Check its data-use terms and your local data law before sending personal or health data.
Chat APIs take a list of messages with roles, plus usually a system prompt that sets the model's overall behaviour.
Messages alternate between "user" (the person or your app) and "assistant" (the model). Earlier assistant turns can be included to give context.

manas.q: What are the two main message roles in a chat API?

children.note: Instructions that frame the whole conversation: the assistant's role, audience, tone, rules and output format. It is set by the developer, not the end user.

manas.q: What is a system prompt for?

children.note: Be specific about the task, give examples of good output, and say what to do when unsure. Put long reference documents in clearly marked sections.
Showing two or three example inputs and ideal outputs in the prompt often improves consistency more than extra rules.
Text from users, web pages or files may contain instructions that try to override yours. Treat outside content as data and limit what the model is allowed to do.

manas.q: What is prompt injection?

children.note: Generation settings change how the model picks each next token.
Low temperature (near 0) makes output more focused and repeatable; higher values make it more varied and creative, and more error-prone.

manas.q: What does lowering temperature do?

children.note: Sets the most tokens the model may generate. Too low cuts answers off mid-sentence; the response tells you if it stopped for this reason.
Top-p limits choices to the most likely tokens making up a share p of probability. Stop sequences end output when a chosen string appears.
Streaming sends text back piece by piece as it is generated, so users see the answer start quickly instead of waiting.
Models read and write tokens, small pieces of text. Billing, speed and limits are all counted in tokens.
A token is a word or word piece. In English one token is roughly three-quarters of a word on average; other languages, such as Swahili or Hindi, often need more tokens per word.

manas.q: Roughly how many English words is one token?

children.note: Providers charge per million tokens, with output tokens usually priced higher than input. Check current prices; they change often.

manas.q: Which usually costs more per token: input or output?

children.note: The maximum tokens a model can consider at once, prompt plus answer. Long documents may need to be split or summarised to fit.
Use a smaller model for simple tasks, shorten prompts, cache repeated prompt parts where offered, and batch non-urgent jobs.
APIs cap requests and tokens per minute. Handle 429 and 5xx errors by retrying with exponential backoff.
Tool use lets the model ask your code to run a function, such as checking a database or the weather, and then use the result.
You send a name, description and JSON Schema of inputs for each tool. Good descriptions are what let the model choose correctly.
The model replies with a tool call and arguments; your code runs the function and sends the result back; the model continues, possibly calling more tools.

manas.q: In function calling, who actually runs the function?

children.note: The model can pick wrong arguments. Check inputs, and require human confirmation for anything risky like payments or sending messages.

manas.q: Why should tool arguments be validated?

children.note: An agent is a loop where the model repeatedly plans, calls tools and reads results until a goal is met. More autonomy means more need for limits and logging.
MCP is an open standard, introduced by Anthropic in November 2024, for connecting models to tools and data sources in a common way; other major providers adopted it.
Apps often need data, not prose: JSON that code can parse reliably.
Describe the exact fields and types you want and give an example. Many APIs offer a JSON mode or schema option that constrains output.

manas.q: How do you get machine-readable output from an LLM?

children.note: Parse the output and check it with a schema library such as Pydantic or JSON Schema. Retry or fall back if it fails.
A common use is pulling fields from messy text, such as patient name, date and drug from a referral letter, into a clean record.
Defining a tool whose input schema is the record you want is another way to get well-formed structured output.
LLM output varies and can be confidently wrong, so test it systematically rather than trusting a few good demos.
Collect realistic inputs with expected outputs or grading notes, including hard and edge cases from real users.

manas.q: What is the first step in evaluating an LLM app?

children.note: Exact match, regular expressions, schema validation and code tests work well when there is a clear right answer.
Another LLM can grade answers against a rubric. It scales well, but check its grades against human judgement on a sample.
For high-stakes uses such as health or law, experts must review samples, and outputs should not be acted on unchecked.
Changing the prompt, model or settings can fix one case and break others. Rerun the full test set each time.

manas.q: Why rerun evaluations after changing a prompt?

children.note: Models can invent facts, citations and numbers. Ground answers in supplied documents and ask the model to say when it does not know.
Some models publish their weights, so you can run them on your own computer or server instead of calling a cloud API.
Open-weight models release their trained parameters for download. Licences vary in what use, change and redistribution they allow, and training data is often not released.

manas.q: What does "open weights" mean?

children.note: Ollama is open-source software, released in 2023, for downloading and running language models locally, with a command line and a local REST API.
Families such as Llama, Mistral, Gemma and Qwen publish open-weight versions in several sizes.
Data stays on your machine, there is no per-token bill, and it works offline. Useful where internet is unreliable or data is sensitive.

manas.q: Name two reasons to run a model locally.

children.note: Small local models are usually less capable than the largest hosted ones, and need a capable GPU or lots of memory. Quantised versions trade some quality for size.
Short explainers and hands-on tutorials on building with LLMs.
